title: Customer Experience (CX) Professional
tagline: Design, deliver and measure experiences that customers anywhere remember for the right reasons, and build the culture that keeps them coming back.
description:
Customers everywhere now compare your branch, your helpline and your app with the best experience they have had anywhere. This certification teaches the full CX discipline in practical terms.

- **Why experience matters:** the difference between customer service and customer experience, the economics of loyalty, moments of truth and the role of emotion.
- **Understanding customers:** voice of the customer, personas, journey maps, pain points and service blueprints.
- **Delivering excellence:** empathetic communication in the customer's language, handling complaints and difficult customers, service recovery and consistent omnichannel service across branch, contact centre, chat and app.
- **Measuring what matters:** calculating and interpreting NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution, closing the loop and avoiding metric gaming.
- **Leading a CX culture:** service standards, employee experience, empowerment, complaint handling in regulated sectors under international principles, continuous improvement and building the business case.

The story follows an international bank across cities from London to Nairobi, and every session includes real, well-documented cases from around the world. Each session ends with a scored test. The final exam is demanding and includes calculations, so plan to practise.
audience: Frontline staff in branches, stores, hotels, clinics and contact centres who deal with customers every day
Back-office and operations staff whose processes shape what customers experience
Team leads and supervisors responsible for service quality and complaint handling
CX, service quality and complaint-management managers in banks, telecoms, insurers, retailers and service firms worldwide
Professionals preparing to move into a customer experience or quality role
outcomes: Explain the difference between customer service and customer experience and estimate the financial value of loyalty
Map a customer journey and a service blueprint to locate pain points and their root causes
Handle complaints and difficult customers with a structured, empathetic recovery approach across channels and languages
Calculate and correctly interpret NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution, and spot gamed metrics
Design a closed-loop feedback process that fixes both individual cases and underlying causes
Apply international complaint-handling principles and describe escalation routes in regulated sectors in several countries
Build a practical CX improvement plan and business case that leadership will fund

quest.name: The Lanterns of Orvana
quest.premise: Orvana Bank serves customers from London to Nairobi, Dubai, Singapore and Toronto. On its Lantern Board every customer is a light that dims each time the bank lets them down. You have been appointed Experience Warden. Pass through five stages, from the Gate of First Impressions to the Citadel of Lanterns, learning to see the bank through customers' eyes, to repair broken promises, to read the true signals of loyalty and to build a culture that keeps every lantern burning.

badge.description: Awarded to professionals who proved they can design, deliver, measure and lead customer experience to a demanding international standard.

cast.name: Wanjiru Kamau
cast.role: CX data analyst who runs the Lantern Board, Nairobi

cast.name: Lukas Becker

cast.name: Rosa Almeida

sessions.title: What CX Really Is: Loyalty, Moments of Truth and Emotion
sessions.summary: Learn what separates customer experience from customer service, why loyal customers are worth so much more than new ones, which moments decide how customers feel, and how emotion shapes what they remember.
objectives: Distinguish customer experience from customer service and explain who owns each
Estimate customer lifetime value and show how small retention gains change it
Identify moments of truth in a customer relationship and prioritise them
Explain how emotion, effort and the peak-end effect shape what customers remember

cards.title: Day one at the gate
cards.setting: Orvana Bank head office, London. Your first morning as Experience Warden. A wall screen glows with thousands of tiny lanterns, one per customer.

lines.text: Welcome, Warden. Every lantern on Wanjiru's board is a customer of Orvana Bank. Bright means they trust you. Dim means they are quietly packing their bags.
See this one flickering? Rosa Almeida, a retired teacher in Toronto, with us for 22 years. Two branch visits and three helpline calls this month alone.
And look at her survey: five out of five for staff courtesy. Everyone she met was polite. Everyone.
(WhatsApp voice note) Querido, my pension came, but the machine says my card is blocked. I had to borrow from my neighbour. My son says move to his bank. Maybe he is right.
Courtesy at 92%. The contact centre is doing its job. CX is their department, isn't it? I don't see why Finance should fund anything.
Is it their department, Lukas? Warden, your first mission: by the end of today, tell him why a customer who loves our staff is still walking towards the gate.

cards.title: Service is a department. Experience is everything.

scenes.heading: Customer service
scenes.narration: Customer service is the help a customer receives when they ask for it: the agent on the phone, the officer at the counter, the assistant processing a return. It is mostly reactive, and a service team owns it.

scenes.heading: Customer experience
scenes.narration: Customer experience is the customer's total perception of you, built from every interaction across the whole relationship. The advert, the form, the SMS alerts, the statement, the app update, and yes, the helpline.

scenes.heading: Built backstage
scenes.narration: Most of those moments are designed by people who never speak to a customer: product, IT, operations, finance, legal and marketing. So CX needs shared ownership across every function, led from the top.

scenes.heading: Every call is a clue
scenes.narration: If a customer has to call you, something in the experience may already have failed. A brilliant agent can soften a confusing statement. Only a redesigned statement removes the pain.

scenes.heading: Rosa's real problem
scenes.narration: Rosa never had a courtesy problem. A dormancy flag, a missing reminder and a separate card team failed her. Great service is one ingredient of great experience, but it cannot cover a broken process for ever.

cards.title: Service versus experience
cards.caption: High courtesy scores can hide a broken journey. CX looks at the whole goal, such as 'get my pension and get on with my day'.

items.label: Scope
items.right: The entire relationship

items.label: Timing
items.left: Mostly after a need or problem
items.right: Before, during and after purchase

items.label: Owner
items.right: Every function, led from the top

items.label: Key question
items.right: Would this customer choose us again?

items.label: Typical fix
items.left: Kinder agents for a confusing bill
items.right: A bill nobody needs to call about

cards.question: A bank's call-centre agents score very highly on courtesy, yet complaints about a confusing loan statement keep rising. What is the most accurate CX diagnosis?
options: Agents need more empathy training so callers feel better about the statement
The statement design is an experience problem that service excellence alone cannot remove
Courtesy scores are unreliable and should be removed from the quality form
The call centre should be given ownership of the statement design
cards.explanation: The pain comes from the statement, which product and operations own. Great agents can soften it, but only a redesign removes the reason to call. More empathy training treats a symptom, and handing the design to the call centre does not create the shared, cross-functional ownership CX needs.

cards.title: Loyalty in money terms: customer lifetime value
cards.body:
CX earns a seat in the boardroom when you speak in money. The key idea is **customer lifetime value (CLV)**: the profit a customer brings over the whole relationship.

- **Churn = 1 − retention.** Keep 80% a year and churn is 20%.
- **Expected relationship (years) ≈ 1 ÷ churn.** 1 ÷ 0.20 = 5 years.
- **CLV ≈ annual profit per customer × expected years.**

It ignores discounting and spending growth, so treat it as a rough guide, not a valuation.

**Why loyalty pays more than the maths shows:**
- Acquisition costs (ads, commissions, KYC) are already paid.
- Loyal customers buy more and cost less to serve.
- They recommend you, and in many markets advice from family and friends drives choices of bank, school and insurer.
- They forgive the odd mistake.

cards.title: Five points of retention, a third more value
cards.caption: Wanjiru's numbers for a typical Orvana Bank retail customer earning USD 120 a year in profit, plus one famous study.

items.label: Churn at 80% retention
items.detail: Churn = 1 − 0.80. One customer in five leaves each year.

items.label: CLV today
items.detail: USD 120 × 5 years.

items.label: CLV at 85% retention
items.detail: 120 × 6.67 ≈ 800. Five retention points add about 33% to each customer's value.

items.label: Across 200,000 customers
items.detail: USD 200 extra per customer × 200,000. Multiply the gain per customer, not the new total CLV.

items.label: Real case: Bain study, 1990
items.detail: Reichheld and Sasser (HBR, 1990): cutting customer defections by 5% raised profits by 25% to 85% across the industries they studied.

cards.question: A microfinance lender earns USD 80 a year in profit per borrower and keeps 75% of borrowers each year. Using CLV ≈ annual profit × (1 ÷ churn), what is the approximate lifetime value of a borrower?
options: USD 60
USD 107
USD 320
USD 240
cards.explanation: Churn = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, so the expected relationship is 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 years, and CLV ≈ 80 × 4 = USD 320. USD 60 multiplies profit by retention, and USD 107 divides profit by retention instead of churn.

cards.front: High retention always means loyal customers.
cards.back: Myth. Customers who stay only because switching is hard, like salary accounts chosen by an employer, are captive. Check products held, share of wallet and NPS too.

cards.front: What is real loyalty?
cards.back: Behaviour (staying and buying more) plus attitude (preferring you and recommending you).

cards.front: Captive customers + an easy exit = ?
cards.back: A sudden exodus. If the employer moves payroll to another bank, captive salary customers can leave with it overnight.

cards.front: Give the best offers only to new customers.
cards.back: Risky. Long-standing customers refused the same deal learn that loyalty earns nothing. Ask: what will our existing customers think when they see this advert?

cards.front: Retention 90% → 92%. How long does a customer stay?
cards.back: Churn falls from 10% to 8%: 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 years becomes 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5 years. Two points of retention, 25% longer relationships.

cards.front: What makes a CLV case believable to Finance?
cards.back: Stated assumptions, a link to real churn evidence (for example, complainers churn twice as fast) and a pilot with a control group.

cards.title: Rosa's moments of truth
cards.caption: A moment of truth is a point where the customer forms or changes their opinion of you in a way that is hard to reverse.

items.label: First impression
items.detail: She opens her salary account. A manager offers her a seat and remembers her name next time. She judges fast, then looks for proof.

items.label: Moment of need
items.detail: Pension day, card blocked, money borrowed from a neighbour. Stakes and emotions are high, and she is watching closely.

items.label: Moment of decision
items.detail: Her son urges her to move to his bank. Twenty-two years of experience turns into a stay-or-leave choice.

cards.title: Real case: SAS and 50 million moments of truth
cards.body:
In 1981 Jan Carlzon became chief executive of Scandinavian Airlines (SAS), which was losing money. In his book *Moments of Truth* (English edition, 1987) he explained the idea behind its turnaround.

- SAS carried about **10 million** passengers a year. Each met roughly **five** employees, for about **15 seconds** each time.
- That made about **50 million moments of truth** a year: brief contacts in which customers decided whether SAS was the right choice.
- Those moments belonged to check-in agents, cabin crew and baggage staff, not senior managers. So Carlzon pushed authority to the front line and asked managers to support them rather than control them.

SAS returned to profit in the early 1980s and became widely known for its service.

**Lesson for you:** list the brief contacts where your customers judge you, and ask who controls each one. It is usually someone far from the boardroom.

cards.title: Name that moment of truth
cards.prompt: Sort each situation into the kind of moment of truth it is.

items.text: A customer's first visit to a branch to open an account
The welcome call after a new health policy is issued
The first bill on a new postpaid package
A card blocked by a fraud alert while paying for medicines late at night
Cashless approval at the hospital desk as a parent is admitted
An international transfer for a family wedding stuck two days before the event
Car insurance renewal arrives alongside a rival's cheaper quote
A customer's son urges her to move her pension account to his bank

cards.title: How to find the moments that matter
cards.body:
Budgets are limited, so find the handful of moments that drive loyalty and design them deliberately.

- **Where complaints and repeat contacts cluster.**
- **What customers remember**, good and bad. Memories point to moments of truth.
- **Where churn jumps.** At one health insurer, members whose first claim took over 30 days lapsed at 45%, against 15% when it took under 10 days. The first claim is the moment to fix, not the renewal discount.
- **Where stakes are high:** money, health, family, deadlines, public embarrassment.

Polished marble floors do not help a customer stranded at a petrol station by a blocked card.

scenes.heading: Memories, not spreadsheets
scenes.narration: Customers do not keep a record of every minute they spent with you. They keep memories, and memories are shaped by emotion.

scenes.heading: The peak
scenes.narration: The peak-end effect: people judge an experience largely by its most intense moment, good or bad, and by how it ended, not by the total time or the average minute.

scenes.heading: Design the ending
scenes.narration: A long wait that ends with a clear summary and a confirmed next step is often remembered better than a short visit that ends with 'nothing can be done'. Endings are cheap to improve.

scenes.heading: Remove the worst peak first
scenes.narration: One humiliating moment, like being told about a bounced payment in front of a queue, can outweigh many pleasant ones. Fix that before you add any sparkle.

scenes.heading: Effort hurts, even when the outcome is right
scenes.narration: Repeating details, being transferred twice, filling the same form again: high effort creates frustration even when the card works perfectly in the end.

scenes.heading: Dignity is part of the product
scenes.narration: Who is greeted first, whether an elder is offered a seat, whether you speak in a language and tone the customer is comfortable with: customers in every culture notice, and remember.

cards.title: Real case: the colonoscopy studies
cards.body:
Physician Donald Redelmeier and psychologist Daniel Kahneman tested the peak-end effect in hospitals.

- **1996 study:** patients rated their pain every minute during a colonoscopy, then rated the whole procedure afterwards. Their overall memory followed the **worst moment and the final moments**, while the length of the procedure made little difference.
- **2003 trial:** with about **680 patients**, doctors added a few extra, milder minutes at the end of the procedure for half of them. That group remembered the procedure as less unpleasant and was somewhat more likely to come back for a later check.

**Lesson for you:** a longer experience with a gentle ending can be remembered better than a shorter one with a painful finish. Remove the worst peak and design the ending before chasing small cuts in total time.

cards.title: Same failure, different ending
cards.caption: Two families at a guesthouse in Cape Town lose hot water for three hours. The negative peak is identical; the ending decides the memory.

items.label: At check-out
items.right: Duty manager names the problem and the impact on small children

items.label: What was said
items.right: "I am sorry. That is hard with little ones."

items.label: Remedy
items.right: Breakfast charge removed; faulty valve replaced

items.label: Small gesture
items.right: A box of local biscuits for the road

items.label: Review
items.right: 4 stars: "they owned it and fixed it"

cards.question: Under the peak-end effect, which change is likely to improve how customers remember a 20-minute visit to a busy service counter, at the lowest cost?
options: Cutting the visit from 20 to 17 minutes by adding one more counter
Repainting the waiting hall in brighter colours
Sending a satisfaction survey the next day
Ending each visit with a clear confirmation of what happens next and when
cards.explanation: Endings carry heavy weight in memory and a clear confirmed next step costs almost nothing. Shaving three minutes costs a whole counter and barely changes the memory; repainting does not touch the peak or the end; a survey only measures.

cards.title: Read the emotion in their words
cards.prompt: Match each idea to the customer words that reveal it.

pairs.right: "This is the third time I am explaining, all over again."
"The money is sent but nobody can tell me where it is. Nobody listens."
"They announced my bounced payment in front of the whole queue."
"I only keep this account because my employer pays my salary into it."
"My renewal is next week and another insurer has quoted less."
"The wait was long, but she explained everything at the end, so I left happy."

cards.title: The money question
cards.setting: Fourth-floor meeting room, 5 pm. Lukas has a calculator, a cup of coffee and very little patience.

lines.text: So customers like our staff but hate our processes. Fine. Fixing dormancy reminders and card unblocking costs money. Why should I care about one retired teacher?
Because she isn't one. Customers who complained about blocked cards last year churned at almost twice the average rate.
And every one of them used words like 'third time' and 'nobody helps'. My agents hear it all day.
Warden, Lukas speaks money. This is your moment of truth with him. How will you make the case?

cards.title: Pitching loyalty to Finance
cards.situation: You have Wanjiru's data: average annual profit USD 120 per customer, retention 80% (CLV ≈ USD 600), and evidence that blocked-card complainers churn at twice the average rate. You think a fix to dormancy reminders and card unblocking could lift retention. Lukas has ten minutes. What do you put in front of him?

choices.text: Assume the fix lifts retention to 95% so the number looks big enough to win the room
choices.outcome: Lukas checks the maths, sees no evidence for a 15-point jump and stops reading. Inflated assumptions destroy credibility for this case and the next one.

choices.text: Show the CLV estimate with your assumptions stated, link it to the churn evidence, and propose a two-region pilot with a control group
choices.outcome: Lukas nods. The logic is clear, the claim is modest and the risk is small. He approves the pilot because its effect will be measured, not assumed.

choices.text: Play Rosa's voice note and talk about delighting customers, without numbers
choices.outcome: The room is moved for a moment, but Lukas asks, 'And what does it return?' Stories open hearts; numbers and evidence open budgets. You need both.

choices.text: Quote a global hotel-industry benchmark showing loyalty pays
choices.outcome: Lukas points out that hotels in another country tell him nothing about Orvana Bank's customers. Benchmarks can support a case but never replace your own evidence.

cards.question: A telecom keeps 95% of the staff on a large employer's corporate SIM bundle, but most of them use a rival's second SIM for data, and their NPS is −20. The employer is reviewing the contract. What is the most accurate reading?
options: They are loyal customers, as the 95% retention shows
Much of the retention is captive, so the base is exposed if the employer switches
They are price-sensitive, so a discount on data will fix it
Retention matters more than NPS, so no action is needed
cards.explanation: High retention with low share of wallet (data goes to a rival) and a negative NPS signals captive behaviour, not loyalty. If the employer changes provider, most of these users will go too. Nothing in the data proves price is the cause.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Gate of First Impressions
items: Customer service is assisted help; customer experience is the total perception across the whole relationship, shaped by every function and led from the top.
CLV ≈ annual profit × (1 ÷ churn), with churn = 1 − retention. Small retention gains create large gains in value.
Captive customers stay because switching is hard; real loyalty combines staying, buying more and recommending. Never punish loyal customers to win new ones.
Focus design effort on moments of truth: first impressions, moments of need and moments of decision.
Customers remember peaks and endings. Remove the worst peak first, design the ending, and cut effort even when the outcome is correct.
Repeated effort, lack of ownership and loss of dignity are the emotions most linked to leaving.

cards.prompt: Think of one journey your customers go through with your organisation. What is its most likely moment of truth, what does the ending feel like for the customer today, and which department actually controls that moment?

quiz.question: Which statement best captures the difference between customer service and customer experience?
options: Customer service covers digital channels such as apps and chat, while customer experience covers branches and stores
Service is assisted help when asked; experience is the total perception formed across every interaction
Customer experience is the marketing team's name for customer service
Customer service is measured by NPS while customer experience is measured by CSAT
quiz.explanation: Service is the assisted, often reactive help a customer receives; experience is the overall perception formed across the entire relationship, including interactions designed by people who never meet customers. The channel split and metric split are both false distinctions.

quiz.question: A broadband provider earns an average annual profit of USD 150 per customer and retains 75% of customers each year. Using the simple CLV estimate taught in this session, what is the approximate lifetime value of a customer?
options: USD 200
USD 450
USD 600
quiz.explanation: Churn = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25, so expected relationship ≈ 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4 years. CLV ≈ 150 × 4 = USD 600. USD 112.50 multiplies profit by the retention rate, and USD 200 divides profit by retention instead of churn.

quiz.question: Sana's card is blocked by a fraud alert while she is paying for medicines at a pharmacy in Manchester late at night. In CX terms, this is best described as:
options: A moment of need, which is a high-stakes moment of truth
A first-impression moment that has little effect once the relationship is established
A moment of decision, because she must decide whether to pay in cash
A routine transaction that is unlikely to shape her view of the bank
quiz.explanation: A blocked card during an urgent purchase is a moment of need: emotions and stakes are high, and the bank's response will strongly shape her opinion. It is not a first impression, and a moment of decision refers to stay-or-leave points such as renewals or competitor offers.

quiz.question: A clinic's patients wait about 40 minutes, which is long, but surveys show that patients who were seen by Dr Farah rate the visit far higher than patients of other doctors with similar waits. Dr Farah ends every consultation by summarising the plan and asking if the patient has any worries. Which idea best explains the difference?
options: Patients rate shorter consultations more highly
Total waiting time is the main driver of how patients remember a clinic visit
The ending of an experience weighs heavily in how it is remembered
Patients cannot judge medical quality, so they rate randomly
quiz.explanation: Waits were similar, so duration does not explain the gap. The peak-end effect does: Dr Farah's clear, caring close shapes the memory of the whole visit. Nothing in the scenario suggests shorter consultations or random ratings.

quiz.question: A telecom operator keeps 90% of its subscribers each year. Management proposes a programme expected to raise retention to 92%. Using expected relationship length ≈ 1 ÷ churn, how does the average customer's expected relationship change?
options: From 9 years to about 11 years
From 10 years to 12.5 years
From 10 years to about 10.2 years
From 1.1 years to about 1.09 years
quiz.explanation: Churn falls from 10% to 8%. 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10 years and 1 ÷ 0.08 = 12.5 years, a 25% increase from just two points of retention. Option C wrongly scales by the retention change; option D divides by retention instead of churn.

quiz.question: Most salary-account holders at a bank keep their savings and car financing with competitors but rarely close the salary account because their employer pays through it. How should the CX team describe these customers?
options: Captive rather than loyal: they stay because switching is hard
Highly loyal, because a high retention rate is the best evidence of loyalty
Detractors, because they use competitors for other products
Advocates, because they have kept the account for years
quiz.explanation: Retention alone does not prove loyalty. These customers stay because the employer chose the bank, while their preference is shown by moving other business elsewhere. Calling them detractors assumes a survey score we do not have; calling them advocates assumes recommendation.

quiz.question: Which of these is the strongest reason why designing the end of an interaction is a cost-effective CX lever?
options: Customers usually forget the beginning of interactions entirely
Regulators only review the final step of a customer journey
Endings are the only part of a journey the company controls
Endings carry heavy weight in memory and can often be improved with little cost
quiz.explanation: The peak-end effect gives endings disproportionate influence on memory, and a clear summary, confirmed next step or small gesture is cheap. Customers do not forget beginnings entirely, and companies control far more than endings.

quiz.question: A retailer launches a campaign offering new loyalty-card holders 20% off for three months. Long-standing customers who ask for the same offer are told it is for new members only. What is the main CX risk?
options: The campaign will be so successful that stores become overcrowded and service quality drops for everyone
New customers will not understand the terms
Existing customers learn that loyalty is not valued, weakening retention of the base
The discount will reduce the CSAT score of new customers
quiz.explanation: Rewarding only new customers signals to existing ones that their loyalty earns nothing, which can push them to switch and undercuts the more profitable base. The other options are minor or unrelated to the core risk.

quiz.question: During a review of complaint transcripts, which group of customer phrases is the strongest warning sign of churn risk?
options: "Third time I am calling", "nobody takes ownership", "I felt embarrassed"
"Please send me the full details by email", "what are your branch timings on Saturday?"
"Is there a discount on this package", "can I upgrade"
"Thank you for your help", "I will wait for the SMS"
quiz.explanation: Repeated effort, lack of ownership and loss of dignity are the emotional signals most strongly linked to leaving. The other groups are routine requests, buying signals or positive signals.

quiz.question: A CX lead estimates that improving retention from 80% to 85% raises CLV from USD 600 to about USD 800. The finance head asks why the case should be trusted. Which response best strengthens the case?
options: Increase the assumed retention gain to ten points so the numbers look more convincing
State the assumptions, link the fix to churn evidence and propose a pilot with a control group
Remove the numbers and present customer quotes and complaint stories instead, since CX is about emotion
Argue that every leading company invests in CX, so the bank must too
quiz.explanation: Credible CX cases show assumptions, connect the proposed fix to observed behaviour, and test the effect with a pilot and control group. Inflating assumptions damages credibility; quotes and benchmarks support a case but do not replace evidence.

sessions.title: Understanding Customers: Voice, Personas, Journeys and Blueprints
sessions.summary: Learn to listen to customers systematically, build personas based on real needs, map journeys from the customer's point of view, trace pain points to root causes and use service blueprints to see what happens behind the counter.
objectives: Design a voice-of-the-customer programme that combines solicited, unsolicited and operational data
Build needs-based personas that avoid stereotypes
Map a current-state customer journey and identify pain points and opportunities
Use root-cause tools and service blueprints to locate where and why journeys fail

cards.title: The quiet district
cards.setting: The Bazaar of Voices, Orvana's analytics hub in Nairobi. Wanjiru has split the Lantern Board by country, and the Kuala Lumpur branches glow suspiciously bright.

lines.text: Look at Kuala Lumpur. Almost no written complaints. Those branches must be our best. Let's copy whatever they're doing.
Same number of customers as London, a fifth of the complaints. But dormant accounts and card blocks are just as high there.
I never complained either, you know. Complain to a young boy at the counter, in front of everyone? Too embarrassing. I simply decided to leave.
My agents hear the same three problems every single day. Nobody has ever asked us what they are.
Silence is not satisfaction, Warden. This stage is about listening properly. So: where do we listen first, and how do we find out why Rosa's lantern dimmed?

scenes.heading: Solicited: what you ask
scenes.narration: Solicited feedback is what you ask for: surveys, interviews, focus groups, panels. Transactional surveys follow one interaction and help fix processes and coach teams. Relationship surveys check overall loyalty at regular intervals.

scenes.heading: Unsolicited: what they say anyway
scenes.narration: Unsolicited feedback arrives without being asked: complaints, compliments, app-store reviews, social posts, WhatsApp voice notes, comments to tellers, call recordings. It is often more honest, and more emotional.

scenes.heading: Operational: what they do
scenes.narration: Behaviour tells you what customers never report: repeat calls, abandoned app steps, dormant accounts, policy lapses, prepaid users who stop recharging. Funnel data shows exactly where they drop out.

scenes.heading: Combine them
scenes.narration: Behaviour shows where. Interviews and watching real users try a step show why. To understand lapses, combine lapse data by segment, interviews with people who actually left, and their complaint and claim records.

scenes.heading: Listen in their language
scenes.narration: Offer surveys and complaint routes in the languages your customers actually use, and ask frontline staff every week what customers struggled with. Low complaint volume can mean poor access or politeness, not happiness.

scenes.heading: The real test
scenes.narration: Numbers tell you where; words tell you why. And a voice-of-the-customer programme is judged not by how much data it collects, but by how many changes it causes.

cards.title: Which kind of voice?
cards.prompt: Sort each source into solicited feedback, unsolicited feedback or operational data.

items.text: SMS survey sent after a branch visit
Twice-yearly relationship survey
Focus group with first-time savers in Nairobi
One-star app-store review about login failures
Angry voice note on the bank's WhatsApp
A comment made to a teller at the counter
60% of loan applicants abandon the app at income verification
Prepaid users who stop recharging after two months
One customer calling three times about the same cheque book

cards.question: A telecom company's complaint volumes are low, but monthly data shows that many prepaid customers stop recharging after their first two months. What does this pattern most suggest?
options: Prepaid customers are satisfied, as shown by low complaints
The company should stop measuring complaints
Operational data is revealing a problem customers are not reporting through complaints
The pattern is normal and needs no investigation
cards.explanation: Behaviour often exposes problems customers never report. Low complaints may reflect reluctance or poor access, not satisfaction. Dropping complaint data goes too far; the right move is to combine sources and investigate the drop-off.

cards.title: Real case: Domino's hears the harshest voices
cards.body:
By 2009 Domino's Pizza in the US faced feedback it could not ignore. Taste tests, customer comments and online posts were blunt: some customers said the crust tasted like cardboard.

- Instead of defending the product, the company **rebuilt its pizza recipe** and relaunched it in late 2009.
- Its advertising showed **real customer criticism on screen**, including focus-group comments, and the company's own staff reacting to it.
- The company told the public it had listened, and it reported strong US sales growth in 2010.

**Lesson for you:** feedback is most valuable when it is uncomfortable. Domino's combined what customers said (complaints, comments, focus groups) with taste testing, then fixed the root cause, the product itself, instead of polishing the message about it.

cards.front: Leading question
cards.back: "How satisfied were you with our quick service?" assumes it was quick. Ask neutrally: "How satisfied were you with the time it took?"

cards.front: Double-barrelled question
cards.back: "Rate the speed and friendliness of our staff." A customer who found staff friendly but slow cannot answer. One idea per question.

cards.front: Wrong timing
cards.back: Surveying a motor claim on the day it is registered measures hope, not experience. Survey after settlement, with an optional short pulse at registration.

cards.front: Poor translation
cards.back: A literal translation of an English scale into Arabic, Portuguese or Urdu can change its meaning. Test the wording with real customers before launch.

cards.front: Too long
cards.back: Completion collapses after a few questions on a phone screen. Ask only what you will act on.

cards.front: Survey for coaching a branch team
cards.back: A short transactional survey sent automatically after the visit and linked to that branch. Annual relationship surveys are too slow and too broad for coaching.

cards.title: Real case: Intuit's "Follow Me Home"
cards.body:
Software company Intuit, maker of Quicken, TurboTax and QuickBooks, has long sent its people to watch customers use its products in their own homes and offices. It calls the practice **Follow Me Home**, and founder Scott Cook championed it from the company's early years.

- Staff **observe quietly**: where people hesitate, which workarounds they use, which notes sit beside the screen.
- Observation shows what surveys miss, because customers rarely mention a workaround they no longer notice.
- Intuit has credited customer research of this kind with product ideas, including noticing that many people were using its household-finance software to run small businesses, a need it went on to serve with QuickBooks.

**Lesson for you:** behaviour shows where, words show why, and watching shows what nobody thought to say. Ask permission, watch real tasks, and feed what you see into personas and journey maps.

cards.title: Personas built on needs, not stereotypes
cards.body:
A **persona** is a short, realistic profile of a group of customers who share goals, needs and behaviours. It lets teams design for real people instead of an imaginary 'average customer'.

**Include:** a name and context, goals, needs, behaviours (channels, digital comfort, who helps them decide), frustrations and fears, and a real quote.

**Rules that make personas work:**
- **Build from evidence:** interviews, observation, survey and behavioural data. Personas brainstormed in a meeting room reflect the team's assumptions.
- **Segment by need, not demographics.** "Males 18–25" says nothing about goals. A 55-year-old market trader in Lagos may be more digital than a 30-year-old office worker.
- **Avoid stereotypes** about women, elders or rural customers. Let the data speak.
- **Keep it small:** three to six personas.
- **Use them** in design reviews: "Could Rosa do this on her phone?"

cards.title: Persona: the careful pensioner
cards.body:
Wanjiru's team interviewed 20 pension customers in Toronto and Mississauga. Transaction data showed about a third of pension accounts fit this pattern.

**Rosa, 66, retired teacher.**
- **Goal:** get her pension on time every month without fuss or embarrassment.
- **Needs:** certainty that money has arrived; help in Portuguese for anything complicated; warning before anything changes on her account.
- **Behaviours:** WhatsApp daily; cautious with the banking app; her son set it up; visits the branch when unsure.
- **Frustrations:** "Nobody told me the account would be blocked." Being asked for documents she did not bring.
- **Fears:** fraud calls pretending to be the bank; pressing the wrong button and losing money.

**Design ideas:** a proactive SMS in her preferred language when the pension lands; a warning before an account is marked dormant; a printed and WhatsApp document checklist; staff who help her use the app step by step rather than doing it for her.

cards.title: Walking in Rosa's shoes
cards.setting: An Orvana Bank branch on Dundas Street, Toronto, on the first working day of the month. You queue as a customer, notebook in hand.

lines.text: You walk the journey that pensioners like Rosa face when an account goes dormant: ATM, helpline, branch. Wanjiru times every step. Omar pulls the call logs.
For these customers it's three days between the branch visit and the card working again. Most call us twice in that gap, just to ask: 'Has anything happened?'
The unblock itself takes four hours of work. The rest is silence. She heard nothing from us at all.
Waiting with no news is the worst part. I keep thinking: have they forgotten me? Is my pension safe?
Then that's what goes on the map, Warden. Not our org chart: her steps, her feelings, her waits.

cards.title: Journey map: get my pension this month
cards.caption: A current-state map for pensioners like Rosa whose account goes dormant, built from 20 interviews, call logs and timings. The deepest dip is the silent wait.

items.label: Pension credited
items.detail: Feeling: calm. Pain: no SMS tells her it arrived, or that the account is flagged dormant.

items.label: ATM declines card
items.detail: Feeling: shock and embarrassment. Pain: no explanation on screen.

items.label: Calls the helpline
items.detail: Feeling: frustrated. Pain: transferred twice, repeats her story each time.

items.label: Visits the branch
items.detail: Feeling: tired. Pain: asked for an ID document nobody mentioned on the phone.

items.label: Waits for unblock
items.detail: Feeling: anxious. Pain: three days of silence; calls twice to ask.

items.label: Card works again
items.detail: Feeling: relieved but hurt. Opportunity: confirm, apologise, prevent it happening again.

cards.title: Journey maps that change things
cards.body:
A **customer journey map** shows the steps a customer takes to reach a goal, from their point of view. Typical layers: **stages, customer actions, touchpoints and channels, thoughts and feelings (an emotion curve), pain points and opportunities.**

**What separates a useful map from a poster:**
- **Start from the customer's goal**, not your internal departments.
- **Map the current state first, with evidence**: interviews, call and complaint data, timings, mystery shopping. A map built only from what managers believe is a map of assumptions.
- **One persona per map.** A first-time borrower and a premium client live different journeys.
- **Include the waits.** Silence between touchpoints is where anxiety grows. Often the fix is not a faster backend but proactive updates at each milestone.
- **Involve the people who do the work.**
- **End with owned actions**: prioritised pain points, an owner and a date for each.

cards.question: A car-financing journey map shows customers wait nine working days for approval with no updates, and they call the branch repeatedly. Interviews say the silence feels worse than the delay. What is the best first improvement?
options: Hire more branch staff to answer the status calls
Send proactive SMS updates at key milestones during the wait
Tell customers at application that calling will not speed things up
Remove the wait stage from the journey map, since it has no touchpoint
cards.explanation: The pain is uncertainty, not only the time. Milestone updates remove the reason to call, cheaply. More staff only absorbs the symptom, a warning not to call adds anxiety, and waits belong on the map precisely because nothing visible happens there.

cards.title: Wanjiru's Pareto: 1,000 complaints
cards.caption: Sort reasons by volume. A few causes usually drive most of the pain, so start there.

items.label: Dormancy and card blocks
items.detail: 38% of all complaints on its own.

items.label: Card delivery status
items.detail: Top two together: 640 of 1,000 = 64%.

items.label: App login failures
items.detail: Top three: 800 of 1,000 = 80%.

items.label: Fees and others
items.detail: Fee queries 120, other 80. Smaller, and spread across many causes.

cards.question: A card unit's monthly contacts are: PIN reset 2,400; card delivery status 1,600; app login 600; fee queries 300; other 100. What share of all contacts do the top two reasons represent?
cards.explanation: Total = 5,000. PIN reset + card delivery = 4,000, and 4,000 ÷ 5,000 = 80%. 92% is the top three. Fixing just these two reasons would address most of the contact volume, which is the point of Pareto analysis.

cards.title: Five whys: why did Rosa's card stop working?
cards.prompt: Put the chain in order, from the symptom the customer feels down to a root cause someone can own.
steps: Symptom: pensioners' cards are declined at the ATM on pension day
Why? Their accounts were marked dormant, so withdrawals were blocked
Why? Only pension credits arrived; they made no customer-initiated transactions for a long period
Why? Customers were never told that their own activity was needed to keep the account active
Root cause: no reminder process exists for at-risk pension accounts, and nobody owns one

cards.title: Is it really the root cause?
cards.body:
A **pain point** is what the customer feels; a **root cause** is why it happens. You are there when fixing it would help many customers, it has a clear owner, and it explains the pattern in the data.

- **Beware "staff attitude" or "poor agent information".** These are usually symptoms of tools, targets or missing data. Agents can't give cheque-book status if the courier shares no tracking.
- **Don't stop at the customer either.** "Readers can't get into locked homes" leads to a fixable cause: no way to book a reading visit or submit a verified reading.
- **Use a fishbone** to group causes under People, Process, Policy, Technology, Partners and Environment before anyone points a finger.

cards.title: Layers of a service blueprint
cards.caption: A journey map shows what the customer experiences. A blueprint adds what the organisation does to deliver it, so you can see where failures start.

items.label: Physical evidence
items.detail: What the customer sees or receives: SMS, form, receipt, app screen, signage.

items.label: Customer actions
items.detail: The steps the customer takes.

items.label: Frontstage actions
items.detail: What staff or systems do in view of the customer: teller, agent, app.

items.label: Line of visibility
items.detail: Separates what the customer sees (frontstage) from what happens out of sight.

items.label: Backstage actions
items.detail: Hidden staff work: verification, approvals, data entry, card printing.

items.label: Support processes
items.detail: Systems, partners and other teams: core banking, courier, credit bureau, IT.

cards.title: Read the blueprint
cards.prompt: Match each blueprint term to what Wanjiru found behind Orvana Bank's account-opening counter.

pairs.right: Staff re-type the scanned form into a second system, and typos creep in
Original forms sit until the once-a-day courier batch to central operations
The officer says "we'll call you in two days", but no process triggers the call
The welcome SMS and the printed account letter
Central operations verifies the documents and activates the account
The core banking system and the courier partner's portal

cards.title: Fixing the silent wait
cards.situation: The blueprint for Rosa's card unblock shows the work is finished within four hours backstage. But the card status in the app updates only in an overnight batch, and no SMS goes out, so customers see 'blocked' until the next day and call Omar's team to ask. Repeat calls are piling up. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Show the backstage status (received, in progress, done) in the app in near real time, and send an SMS the moment the card works
choices.outcome: Repeat calls drop sharply within weeks. The blueprint showed the delay was in visibility, not processing, and you fixed it at the source.

choices.text: Give agents a reassuring script for status calls
choices.outcome: Callers feel a little better, but they still had to call. You have softened the symptom while the silence that causes it remains.

choices.text: Push the unblock team to finish in two hours instead of four
choices.outcome: The team works harder, but the app still shows 'blocked' until the overnight batch, so customers keep calling. Speed was never the bottleneck.

choices.text: Hire extra agents to absorb the status calls
choices.outcome: Queues shorten, costs rise, and the calls keep coming. More capacity for failure demand is not a fix.

cards.question: In a service blueprint for issuing a replacement debit card, where would "card is printed at the central card unit and dispatched by courier" appear?
options: Physical evidence
Customer actions
Frontstage actions
Backstage actions or support processes, below the line of visibility
cards.explanation: The customer never sees the printing or the dispatch, so these sit below the line of visibility as backstage work and support (the courier partner). The card itself, when it arrives, is physical evidence.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Bazaar of Voices
items: Combine solicited feedback, unsolicited feedback and operational data; behaviour shows where, words show why. Low complaints do not mean satisfaction.
Avoid leading, double-barrelled, long, badly translated or badly timed surveys; use transactional surveys for coaching and relationship surveys for loyalty.
Build three to six needs-based personas from evidence, avoid stereotypes, and use them in design reviews.
Map the current state from the customer's goal with evidence, include the waits, and finish with owned actions.
Use Pareto, five whys and fishbone to move from pain points to root causes that someone can own.
Blueprints reveal fail points, wait points and frontstage promises the backstage cannot keep, below the line of visibility.

cards.prompt: Pick one frequent customer complaint in your area. Apply the five whys honestly. Where did you end up, who owns that root cause, and is it inside or outside your team?

quiz.question: Which of these is an example of unsolicited customer feedback?
options: Responses to an SMS survey sent after a branch visit
Answers from a focus group on a new savings product
A one-star app-store review complaining about login failures
Results of a yearly relationship survey
quiz.explanation: An app-store review is given without the company asking. SMS surveys, focus groups and relationship surveys are all solicited feedback.

quiz.question: An insurer wants to understand why customers lapse after the first policy year. Which combination of VoC inputs would give the most complete picture?
options: Lapse data by segment, interviews with lapsed customers, and complaint and claim records
A detailed relationship survey of current policyholders, repeated every quarter for a full year
Social media monitoring of competitor brands
Agent opinions about why customers lapse
quiz.explanation: Combining behavioural data (who lapses), solicited insight from people who actually left and unsolicited and operational records (complaints, claims) gives the fullest view. Surveying only current customers misses those who left; agent opinion alone is one biased source.

quiz.question: A survey asks: "How satisfied were you with the speed and friendliness of our staff?" What is the main problem with this question?
options: It is leading, because it assumes in advance that the staff were both fast and friendly
It should use a 10-point scale instead of a 5-point scale
It is too short to give useful data
It is double-barrelled, so one rating cannot show which aspect is being judged
quiz.explanation: Speed and friendliness are two different things; a customer who found staff friendly but slow cannot answer accurately. The question does not assume an answer, so it is not leading, and scale length is not the issue.

quiz.question: A digital bank's team proposes three personas: "Males 18–25", "Males 26–40" and "Females 18–40". What is the strongest criticism?
options: There should be at least ten personas
They are demographic bands that say nothing about goals, needs or behaviours
Personas should never include gender
They are acceptable, because demographics are easy to measure and link directly to marketing data
quiz.explanation: Useful personas are based on needs, goals and behaviours shown by evidence. Age-gender bands lump together customers who behave very differently. The number of personas and the presence of demographic details are not the core issue.

quiz.question: A journey map of a mobile package change shows that customers feel most anxious in the 24 hours after requesting the change, when they receive no confirmation and are unsure if they will be charged twice. What is the best first improvement?
options: Speed up the backend so that the package change completes in 12 hours instead of 24 hours
Offer a discount on the next package change
Send instant confirmation and a completion message that explains how billing will work
Add more agents to handle the calls from anxious customers
quiz.explanation: The pain is uncertainty during the wait, not the wait itself. Proactive confirmation and clear billing information address the cause cheaply. A faster backend helps but still leaves silence; more agents only absorb symptoms.

quiz.question: Complaint data for a utility company shows: billing errors 410, late connection 160, rude staff 90, meter reading disputes 260, app issues 80. Using Pareto thinking, which two categories should be tackled first?
options: Rude staff and app issues, because they are the quickest to fix and show visible progress
Late connection and rude staff
All five equally, to show customers every issue matters
Billing errors and meter reading disputes, about two-thirds of the total
quiz.explanation: Total = 1,000. Billing errors (410) plus meter disputes (260) = 670, about 67% of complaints. Pareto analysis directs effort to the few causes driving most volume. They may also share a root cause in meter reading.

quiz.question: A team applies the five whys to repeated calls about delayed cheque books and concludes, "Root cause: call-centre agents give poor information." Why is this probably not the real root cause?
options: Agent behaviour is likely a symptom; the deeper cause may be missing tracking data from the courier
The five whys technique can only be used for IT problems
Agents are never responsible for customer problems
Cheque book delays are caused by the courier company, so they are outside the bank's control and cannot be fixed
quiz.explanation: Stopping at people often misses systemic causes. If agents have no tracking data, better scripts will not help. Agents can contribute to problems, so option C overstates; five whys is not limited to IT.

quiz.question: In a service blueprint for a home loan, a branch officer promises the customer "we will call you within two days with an update", but no process or system exists to trigger that call. What type of problem has the blueprint revealed?
options: A physical evidence problem
A frontstage promise that backstage processes cannot keep
A problem with the customer's actions
A persona design error
quiz.explanation: The promise is made frontstage, but no backstage or support process delivers it, so it will often be broken. Blueprints are designed to expose this kind of gap across the line of visibility.

quiz.question: Which statement about journey maps and service blueprints is correct?
options: Journey maps are used for digital channels such as apps, and blueprints for physical channels such as branches
Blueprints replace the need to talk to customers
Journey maps show internal handovers in detail, while blueprints show only emotions
Journey maps show the customer's experience; blueprints add the activities that deliver it
quiz.explanation: A journey map views the experience from outside; a blueprint extends it to show what the organisation does, visible and invisible, to deliver each step. Both apply to any channel and neither replaces customer research.

quiz.question: A bank's branches in one country receive far fewer written complaints than its branches in a neighbouring country, though customer numbers are similar. A manager concludes the low-complaint branches deliver better service. What is the best response?
options: Agree, and use the low-complaint branches as the benchmark when setting service standards for the whole network
Reduce complaint channels in the higher-complaint country to lower the volume
Treat it as a hypothesis; fewer complaints may reflect access or reluctance, not better service
Ignore complaint data because it is unreliable
quiz.explanation: Complaint volume depends on how easy and culturally acceptable it is to complain, not only on service quality. Check with other sources such as operational data, surveys in local languages and mystery shopping before concluding. Ignoring complaint data entirely goes too far.

sessions.title: Delivering Service Excellence: Empathy, Complaints, Recovery and Omnichannel
sessions.summary: Build the practical skills of excellent service: clear and empathetic communication, a structured way to handle complaints and difficult customers, service recovery that restores trust, bilingual and cultural awareness, and consistent omnichannel service.
objectives: Use active listening, positive language and genuine empathy in the customer's language
Handle a complaint using the five-step ASAAN approach
De-escalate difficult customers while protecting staff dignity and safety
Design service recovery that is fair in outcome, process and treatment
Deliver consistent service across branch, call centre, WhatsApp and app

cards.title: The call that went wrong
cards.setting: Orvana Bank contact centre, Toronto. Omar plays you a recording from yesterday afternoon. A new agent took Rosa's third call.

lines.text: I have explained this twice already! My pension is in the account and I cannot take it out. My rent is due tomorrow.
The agent replies: "Madam, please calm down. Your case is pending with CBS ops for maker-checker. TAT is 48 hours. That's our policy."
Calm down? What is CBS? I am a teacher, young man, not a computer. Nobody in this bank listens.
Every sentence he said was technically true. And every sentence made it worse.
This is the Hall of Mended Promises, Warden. Rosa is coming to the branch tomorrow. When she does, how do we get her lantern back?

scenes.heading: Listen to understand
scenes.narration: Let the customer finish. Take notes. Agents who start solving too early often solve the wrong problem, and the customer has to repeat everything.

scenes.heading: Confirm what you heard
scenes.narration: "So your pension arrived on the first, but the ATM declined your card, and the rent is due tomorrow. Is that right?" It proves you listened and prevents mistakes.

scenes.heading: Plain language
scenes.narration: Drop the internal words: CBS, TAT, maker-checker, 'the case is in the queue'. Say: 'The team that approves this usually takes up to two working days.'

scenes.heading: Lead with what you can do
scenes.narration: Positive, action-focused language starts with the possible. Not 'I can't do anything until Monday', but 'The team is back on Monday; I'm submitting it now so it's first in line.'

scenes.heading: Honest expectations
scenes.narration: Give the realistic time, not the one the customer wants to hear. A missed promise creates a second complaint on top of the first.

scenes.heading: Tone and respect
scenes.narration: Customers judge tone in seconds. Use the customer's name, a respectful title like Mrs Almeida, and the polite form of 'you' where the language has one. In writing, read your message once from the customer's side before sending.

cards.title: Rewrite the reply
cards.prompt: Match each unhelpful line to the plain, positive version that is still accurate.

pairs.right: "The team that approves this usually takes up to two working days."
"Let me connect you to the right person and explain your case to them first."

pairs.left: "I can't change your address without the signed form."
pairs.right: "As soon as the signed form reaches me, I'll update it the same day. Shall I send you the form on WhatsApp?"
"Let me explain how this charge works and what options you have."
"The team is back on Monday; I'm submitting it now so it's first in line."

cards.title: Empathy that is real, not scripted
cards.body:
**Empathy** is understanding how the situation feels for the customer and showing it. It is not **sympathy** (feeling sorry) and not **agreement** (saying the company was wrong). You can empathise even when a policy was correctly applied.

**Three moves:**
1. **Name the situation specifically:** "Your pension is in the account, and the rent is due tomorrow."
2. **Acknowledge the feeling:** "I can see why that is so worrying."
3. **Move to action:** "Let me check exactly what has blocked it, right now."

A stock line like "I understand your frustration", repeated in the same tone and followed by nothing, sounds fake. In any language, warmth comes from specific, sincere words in the customer's own terms, followed by action.

**Limits:** empathy is not false promises, blaming colleagues or a 35-minute call of reassurance that never traces the transfer. Warmth without resolution just adds effort and a repeat call.

cards.question: A customer's car-insurance claim was correctly declined because the driver had no valid licence. The customer is upset. Which response shows empathy without misleading the customer?
options: "I completely agree, the decision is unfair. I will try to get it reversed."
"Sir, the policy is clear. There is nothing more to discuss."
"I understand this is a big financial blow after an accident. Let me explain exactly why it was declined and what options you have."
"I understand your frustration. Please hold."
cards.explanation: It names the specific impact, acknowledges it and moves to a clear explanation and options. The first option agrees falsely and promises what the agent cannot deliver; the second is cold; the last is a stock phrase followed by nothing.

cards.title: LEARN: a complaint structure
cards.caption: Five steps for handling any complaint. The goal is to make resolution easy for the customer and to learn from every case.

items.label: L: Listen and acknowledge
items.detail: Thank them, listen without interrupting, recognise the feeling. Do not defend or explain policy yet.

items.label: E: Explore
items.detail: Open then closed questions; check the record; separate what they want from what happened.

items.label: A: Apologise appropriately
items.detail: Own clear faults plainly. If facts are unclear, regret the trouble without admitting unproven fault. Never blame colleagues.

items.label: R: Resolve together
items.detail: Offer options, agree what happens and by when, act now. If handing over, brief the next person yourself.

items.label: N: Notify and follow through
items.detail: Confirm it worked, log the root cause, and in regulated sectors give the reference and escalation route.

cards.question: An officer checks the system and confirms that the bank's own dormancy process blocked a customer's account without the reminder the bank's policy requires. What kind of apology fits the LEARN approach?
options: Apologise only for the inconvenience, avoiding any admission of fault
Own the bank's mistake plainly and sincerely, without blaming another team
Explain that operations made the error, so the branch is not responsible
Skip the apology and focus on fixing it, since words change nothing
cards.explanation: When the fault is established, an appropriate apology owns it plainly. Hedging is for cases where the facts are still unclear. Blaming another department breaks trust in the whole bank, and skipping the apology makes the fix feel cold.

cards.title: Real case: United Breaks Guitars
cards.body:
In 2008 Canadian musician Dave Carroll watched baggage handlers throwing instruments during a United Airlines connection in Chicago. His guitar arrived broken.

- For many months he tried calls, emails and staff in several places. He was passed from one team to another, and in the end the claim was refused, partly because he had not reported the damage within the airline's time window.
- In 2009 he released a song and video, **United Breaks Guitars**. It was viewed **millions of times within weeks** and drew worldwide press coverage. United contacted him after it spread.

**Lesson for you:** the money at stake was small; he had asked for about **USD 1,200** to cover repairs. What failed was **process and treatment**: no single owner, repeated explanations and a rule applied without listening. A quick, fair recovery at the first complaint would have cost far less than the story that followed.

cards.title: Omar takes the counter
cards.setting: Orvana Bank, Dundas Street branch, Toronto, 10 am. Rosa arrives with her grandson. Omar has come over from the contact centre to meet her himself.

lines.text: Mrs Almeida, thank you for coming in. Please, sit. Having your own pension blocked and borrowing from a neighbour is very upsetting. Tell me everything.
Three calls, two visits! Everyone is polite and nobody does anything!
Omar lets her finish. He asks when she last used the card herself, checks the record, and finds the account was flagged dormant with no reminder ever sent.
I am sorry. We should have warned you before the account was marked inactive. You should never have found out at an ATM.

I can reactivate it right now with your photo ID, so you can withdraw at this counter today. The card usually works within one working day. I will call you tomorrow by 12, either way. Is that all right?
Today? All right. But I am telling you, my son will hear about tomorrow's call.

cards.title: Difficult, abusive or pulling rank?
cards.prompt: Decide how to handle each customer: de-escalate, protect staff from abuse, or stay courteous while the rule stands.

items.text: A caller has been shouting for two minutes about his third billing error this month
A mother in tears because her son's university fee transfer hasn't arrived
"Oh, great service. Third visit this week!"
A caller hurls abusive personal insults at the agent after a loan decline
A caller keeps making suggestive remarks to a female agent
"Do you know who I am? Open my nephew's account today, ID or no ID."
An angry customer demands the bank reverse a correct credit decision on the spot
A customer insists on a waiver above the officer's authority, "right now"

cards.title: De-escalate without giving in
cards.body:
**Do:** lower your voice slightly, let them vent, use their name and title, agree with what is true ("You should have had an SMS"), move to specifics, offer choices ("I can call you back in an hour, or you can wait while I check"), and move to a private desk if needed.

**Never say:** "Calm down." "That's our policy." "You must have done something wrong." "I'm new here." "You should have told us earlier."

**Pulling rank?** Same courtesy, same rules, and offer the fastest compliant route. **Abuse or harassment?** One calm warning, then end the call per policy and record it; in person, call a supervisor or security. Organisations must back staff with a clear policy and debriefs.

cards.title: Service recovery: three kinds of fairness
cards.body:
**Service recovery** is what you do after you fail a customer. Customers judge it on three kinds of fairness:

1. **Fair outcome:** a reasonable result: correction, refund, replacement or compensation in proportion to the harm.
2. **Fair process:** quick, clear, one owner, no chasing, no repeating the story.
3. **Fair treatment:** respect, honesty, empathy and an explanation.

A full refund after five calls fails on process; a refund in 24 hours with a rude remark fails on treatment.

**Principles:** speed matters; **empower the front line** to fix common problems on the spot within limits; **restore the customer fully**, including knock-on costs such as a bounced-cheque charge, and add a gesture for serious inconvenience; **fix the cause.**

**The recovery paradox:** after excellent recovery, a customer can end up more loyal than before. It happens only sometimes, after a one-off, not-too-severe failure, and it vanishes when the failure repeats. Prevention beats recovery.

cards.title: Two outages, two memories
cards.caption: A fibre provider in Nairobi loses service for 30 hours after a contractor cuts a cable. Same failure, very different recovery.

items.label: Fair process
items.left: "Technical team is working"; callers told to restart routers
items.right: SMS and WhatsApp in English and Swahili within two hours, updates every six hours

items.label: Fair treatment
items.right: Took responsibility and named the impact on people working from home

items.label: Fair outcome
items.left: Credit only for persistent complainers, varying by agent
items.right: Automatic pro-rata credit plus two extra days for everyone affected

items.label: Fix the cause
items.right: Cable-marking agreement with the city roads authority

cards.title: Real case: JetBlue's 2007 ice storm
cards.body:
In February 2007 an ice storm hit New York. JetBlue kept passengers on board in the hope of departing, and several aircraft sat on the ground at JFK airport for many hours, some for around ten. Its operation struggled for days afterwards.

- Founder and chief executive David Neeleman **apologised publicly and repeatedly**, in the media and in a letter to customers, without hiding behind the weather.
- Within days JetBlue published a **Customer Bill of Rights** that promised set compensation for delays and cancellations it caused, including long waits on the ground.
- It also worked on the causes, including the communication and crew-scheduling systems that had failed.

**Lesson for you:** fair treatment (a sincere apology), fair outcome (defined compensation) and fair process (clear rules, faster updates) work together. Writing compensation rules in advance also lets staff act quickly the next time.

cards.question: A customer receives a full refund of a wrongly charged USD 45 fee, but only after five calls over three weeks, explaining the issue again each time. Which fairness dimension was weakest?
options: Fair outcome, because the refund was too small
Fair process, because the customer had to chase and repeat themselves
None, because the customer received a full refund
Fair treatment, because the agents were probably rude
cards.explanation: The outcome was fair: a full refund. But chasing, delay and repetition make the process unfair. Nothing suggests rudeness, and a fair outcome alone does not make recovery feel fair.

cards.title: What does Rosa deserve?
cards.situation: The next morning Omar confirms Rosa's card works. You learn more: because she couldn't withdraw on time, her rent was paid late, her landlord charged a CAD 50 late fee, and she had to borrow from a neighbour. The block happened because Orvana Bank never sent the dormancy reminder its own policy requires. As Warden, you design the recovery.

choices.text: Reactivate the card, apologise warmly, and close the case
choices.outcome: Rosa is polite but cool. The bank's mistake still cost her CAD 50 and her dignity with a neighbour. The outcome is incomplete, and nothing stops it happening to the next pensioner.

choices.text: Refund the CAD 50 late fee, write a short apology owning the error, call when promised, and get operations to add dormancy-warning SMS for pension accounts
choices.outcome: Rosa is restored fully, treated with respect and sees the cause fixed. She tells Omar, 'At least you admitted it.' Her lantern steadies. Thousands of pensioners will now be warned in time.

choices.text: Ask her to file a formal complaint with receipts for the late fee; it will be reviewed within 30 days
choices.outcome: An obvious bank error now costs her another month of chasing. The process feels unfair, and her son starts filling in his bank's account form.

choices.text: Send a CAD 250 gift voucher by post without any explanation
choices.outcome: Generous, but it doesn't explain what happened, doesn't fix the cause and feels like a payoff. Money cannot substitute for fair treatment and a real fix.

cards.front: A full refund always fixes the relationship.
cards.back: Myth. A fair outcome with a slow, repetitive process or a rude remark still feels unfair. Customers judge outcome, process and treatment separately.

cards.front: The recovery paradox
cards.back: Excellent recovery after a one-off failure can raise loyalty. When the same failure happens again, the effect disappears, because now it looks systemic.

cards.front: What does 'restore fully' mean?
cards.back: Reverse the error and its knock-on costs: a double debit, the bounced-cheque charge it caused, and a letter for the supplier if the customer's reputation suffered.

cards.front: Full refund in 24 hours, but the agent said 'customers like you always complain'.
cards.back: Fair treatment failed. Disrespect alone can turn a well-resolved case into an angry review.

cards.front: Small waivers need supervisor sign-off taking 25 minutes, and nearly all are approved.
cards.back: Let agents waive up to a set limit, with logging and audit. The approval adds delay, not control.

cards.title: Language, respect and culture
cards.body:
Customers in global cities often move between languages, even in one conversation: Portuguese and English in Toronto, Arabic, English and Hindi or Urdu in Dubai, Swahili and English in Nairobi.

- **Follow the customer's language** where your rules allow. If they write their language in Latin letters (Roman Urdu in Pakistan, Arabic chat script in the Gulf), reply simply in the same style, without jargon.
- **Don't assume** language skills from appearance or accent.
- **No one speaks it?** Find a colleague or an approved interpreter, or help with the form in simple words, and **log the language need** so staffing can be fixed.
- **Respect:** a title, the polite form of 'you', a seat and patience for elders.
- **Privacy and gender:** if a customer hesitates over a sensitive matter, offer a private desk or a colleague of the same gender. Offer; don't assume.
- **Peaks:** month-start and festivals such as Eid, Christmas, Diwali and Lunar New Year. Plan staff and tone.
- **Accessibility** is part of service, not charity.

scenes.heading: Multichannel is not enough
scenes.narration: Multichannel means offering many doors: branch, call centre, WhatsApp, app. Omnichannel means the doors open into the same room, so a customer can start in one channel and finish in another without starting again.

scenes.heading: Shared context
scenes.narration: Rosa told WhatsApp, then the helpline, then the branch, and got three reference numbers. With one shared case view, the officer says: 'I can see you messaged us yesterday,' before asking anything.

scenes.heading: One truth everywhere
scenes.narration: Fees and policies must match in every channel. If the app showed a zero fee and the branch charged USD 3, honour what you quoted, fix the wrong screen at source, and check who else was affected.

scenes.heading: Security is experience
scenes.narration: Fraudsters pose as banks on WhatsApp. Repeat in every channel that you never ask for an OTP, PIN or password, verify your official accounts, and give customers a fast way to block a card.

scenes.heading: Digital, with a hand to hold
scenes.narration: Pushing everyone to the app saves money but can exclude elderly and low-literacy customers. Phase changes in, offer assisted onboarding and simple guides in customers' own languages, and keep an assisted route open.

items.label: Customer history
items.left: Each channel sees only its own contacts
items.right: Every channel sees recent contacts and open cases

items.label: References
items.right: One reference per issue, whatever the channel

items.label: Information
items.left: Fees and answers vary by channel
items.right: Same fees, policies and answers everywhere

items.label: Switching channels
items.right: Start in the app, finish at the branch

items.label: Security
items.right: "We never ask for your OTP" in every channel

cards.question: Which change best moves a bank from multichannel to omnichannel service?
options: Launching a new chatbot on its website
Opening more branches in smaller cities
Extending call-centre hours to 24/7
Giving all channels a shared view of each customer's recent contacts and open cases
cards.explanation: Omnichannel is about channels working as one, which needs shared context. A new chatbot, more branches or longer hours add capacity or channels, which is still multichannel.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Hall of Mended Promises
items: Listen fully, confirm understanding, use plain and positive language, and set honest expectations.
Empathy names the situation, acknowledges the feeling and moves to action; it is not agreement, false promises or endless reassurance.
LEARN: Listen and acknowledge, Explore, Apologise appropriately, Resolve together, Notify and follow through.
Let frustrated customers vent; warn once then end abusive calls; keep rules firm with courtesy when customers pull rank.
Recovery is judged on fair outcome, process and treatment: restore fully, move fast, empower staff within limits and fix the cause.
Omnichannel means shared context, one truth in every channel, security everywhere, and an assisted route for those who need it.

cards.prompt: Recall a recent complaint you handled or observed. Which LEARN step was weakest, and which fairness dimension (outcome, process or treatment) did the customer most likely judge harshly?

quiz.question: An agent says to a caller: "The case is pending with CBS ops for maker-checker, TAT is 48 hours." What is the main communication problem?
options: The agent is too formal
The agent should have transferred the call
The timeline is too short
The agent is using internal jargon the customer is unlikely to understand
quiz.explanation: CBS, maker-checker and TAT are internal terms. Plain language would be: "The team that approves this usually takes up to two days." Formality and timeline length are not the issue here.

quiz.question: A customer is angry that her son's university fee transfer has not reached the university two days before the deadline. Which opening is the strongest example of empathy?
options: "I understand your frustration, madam. May I please have your account number and date of birth to check?"
"With the fee deadline in two days, I can see why this is stressful. Let me trace it now."
"Please don't worry, these things always sort themselves out."
"Transfers can take time. You should have sent it earlier."
quiz.explanation: Option B names the specific situation, acknowledges the feeling and moves straight to action. A is a stock phrase, C gives false reassurance, and D blames the customer.

quiz.question: In the LEARN approach, a branch officer has listened to an upset customer and checked the record, but it is not yet clear whether the bank or the customer made the error. What is the most appropriate apology?
options: Apologise for the trouble caused, without admitting a fault not yet established
Admit that the bank made the error, to calm the customer
Avoid any apology until the investigation is complete, so the bank does not accept liability
Explain that another department is probably responsible
quiz.explanation: LEARN asks for an appropriate apology: sincere regret for the experience without claiming fault that is not established. Admitting unproven fault can mislead; withholding any apology feels cold; blaming another department breaks trust.

quiz.question: A caller at a telecom helpline has been shouting about repeated billing errors for two minutes. What should the agent do first?
options: Interrupt firmly and ask the caller to calm down
Transfer the call to a supervisor immediately, since supervisors have more authority to resolve billing errors
Let the caller finish, acknowledge what went wrong, then move to the details
End the call because the caller is shouting
quiz.explanation: Shouting from frustration is not abuse. Letting the customer vent, then acknowledging and moving to specifics, de-escalates. "Calm down" inflames, transfers add effort, and ending the call is reserved for abusive or threatening behaviour after a warning.

quiz.question: A customer on the phone begins using abusive personal language towards the agent after being told his loan application was declined. According to good practice, what should the agent do?
options: Continue the call silently until the customer finishes
Respond in the same tone so the customer realises it is unacceptable
Reverse the loan decision or promise a review, so that the conflict ends and the customer calms down
Give one calm warning, then end the call per policy and record it if the abuse continues
