quiz.explanation: Staff should not accept abuse. A calm warning gives the customer a chance to continue respectfully; ending the call per policy and recording it protects the agent. Matching the tone escalates; reversing a credit decision under pressure is improper.

quiz.question: An e-commerce company refunds customers fully for damaged deliveries, but only after a 30-day investigation in which customers must email photos twice and are given no updates. Satisfaction with refunds is low. What is the best explanation?
options: The refunds are too small
The process and treatment are perceived as unfair even though the outcome is fair
Customers do not value refunds
Photos should not be requested at all
quiz.explanation: The outcome (a full refund) is fair, but the slow, repetitive, silent process undermines the experience. Requesting a photo once can be reasonable; the problem is duplication, delay and lack of updates.

quiz.question: A hotel guest's room was not ready at check-in for two hours. The hotel apologised, upgraded the room and gave a complimentary dinner. The guest later posts a very positive review. Six months later, the same thing happens again, with the same remedy, and the guest posts a negative review. What does this best illustrate?
options: The guest was being unreasonable the second time
Room upgrades are an ineffective recovery remedy, because guests expect them as standard at good hotels
Recovery can lift loyalty after one failure, but the effect fades when failures repeat
Complimentary dinners should be replaced with cash compensation
quiz.explanation: Excellent recovery may boost loyalty after a one-off failure, but a repeated failure signals that the problem is systemic, so the effect vanishes. This is why prevention and root-cause fixes matter more than recovery gestures.

quiz.question: An elderly customer at a Toronto branch switches to Portuguese after struggling with the English forms. No staff member at the counter speaks Portuguese. What is the best response?
options: Find a Portuguese-speaking colleague or an approved interpreter, or help with the form in simple words, and log the language need
Politely ask the customer to come back with a family member who can read and speak English fluently
Hand the customer the French version of the form instead
Continue in fast English, since most customers in the city speak it
quiz.explanation: Following the customer's language need where possible, and assisting patiently otherwise, reduces effort and respects the customer. Logging the need helps fix the root cause (staffing for customers' languages). The other options shift effort to the customer.

quiz.question: A bank's WhatsApp channel receives messages from customers who say they were contacted by "bank staff" on WhatsApp asking for their OTP. What is the most appropriate CX response?
options: Close the WhatsApp channel to avoid confusion
Ask affected customers to share the OTP they received with the official channel so it can be verified
Leave fraud messaging to the fraud team, since it is not a CX issue
Warn in every channel that OTPs are never requested, verify the official account, offer fast blocking
quiz.explanation: Security is part of the experience. Consistent warnings, a verifiable official account and a quick blocking route protect customers. Closing the channel removes a useful service; asking for OTPs, even officially, reinforces the scam pattern; CX cannot ignore fraud.

quiz.question: A telecom's call-centre agents are allowed to waive late-payment fees only after supervisor approval, which takes an average of 25 minutes per request. Most waivers are below USD 10 and nearly all are approved. What is the best recommendation?
options: Remove the ability to waive fees entirely
Let agents waive fees up to a set limit, with logging and audit
Add more supervisors to the floor so that approvals take five minutes instead of twenty-five
Ask customers to submit waiver requests by email
quiz.explanation: Empowerment within clear limits speeds recovery and reduces effort, while logging and audits manage risk. Since almost all small waivers are approved, the approval step adds delay but little control. More supervisors adds cost; email adds effort.

sessions.title: Measuring CX: NPS, CSAT, CES, FCR and Closing the Loop
sessions.summary: Learn to calculate and interpret the core CX metrics correctly, pair them with operational measures, read changes with statistical caution, close the loop with customers and the organisation, and recognise when metrics are being gamed.
objectives: Calculate NPS, CSAT, CES and first-contact resolution correctly from raw data
Interpret metric changes with attention to sample size, scale and survey design
Design inner-loop and outer-loop processes that turn feedback into action
Recognise metric gaming and design balanced measures that resist it

cards.title: Too good to be true
cards.setting: The Observatory of Signals: Wanjiru's dashboard room at the Nairobi analytics hub. The monthly numbers have just landed, and everyone has crowded in.

lines.text: Look! First-contact resolution up from 70% to 88% in three months. My agents tick 'resolved' on almost every call now.
And the Deira branch in Dubai: 98% CSAT, three months running. Network average is 82%. Give that manager the bonus.
Hmm. Repeat calls within seven days haven't moved at all. And Deira's survey response rate is 4%. Everyone else gets 15%.
(Survey reply, sent the day before Omar met her) Likelihood to recommend Orvana Bank: 3. Reason: "Polite people, broken system. I have told my son to wait one more month."
Signals can lie, Warden, or tell the truth very quietly. Before anyone celebrates or punishes, can you read what these numbers really say?

scenes.heading: Perception
scenes.narration: Perception metrics capture what customers think and feel. NPS: how likely they are to recommend you. CSAT: how satisfied they were. CES: how easy it was.

scenes.heading: Operational
scenes.narration: Operational metrics capture what happened: first-contact resolution, repeat contacts, complaint resolution time, average handling time, queue waits, abandonment.

scenes.heading: Outcome
scenes.narration: Outcome metrics capture business results: retention and churn, products per customer, share of wallet, revenue and cost to serve.

scenes.heading: Link the chain
scenes.narration: The insight is in the links. Customers who needed several contacts give lower effort and NPS scores, and then churn faster. That chain is what convinces Finance to fund a fix.

scenes.heading: Purpose
scenes.narration: Measurement exists to decide what to fix and whether the fix worked. No single metric is enough, and a score nobody acts on is decoration.

items.label: When
items.right: Soon after a specific interaction

items.label: Asks about
items.right: This call, visit, delivery or claim

items.label: Best for
items.right: Fixing processes and coaching staff

items.label: Typical metric
items.right: CSAT, CES, transactional NPS

cards.title: Net Promoter Score in one picture
cards.caption: "On a scale of 0 to 10, how likely are you to recommend us to a friend or colleague?" Fred Reichheld introduced NPS in Harvard Business Review in 2003.

items.label: Promoters
items.detail: Enthusiasts likely to recommend you. Their percentage is added.

items.label: Passives
items.detail: Satisfied but unenthusiastic. They stay in the total, but are neither added nor subtracted.

items.label: Detractors
items.detail: Unhappy customers at risk of leaving and warning others. Their percentage is subtracted.

items.label: NPS = %P − %D
items.detail: Reported as a plain number, such as +32, not as a percentage.

cards.title: Calculating NPS without the classic mistakes
cards.body:
Wanjiru's survey of 500 customers: **190 promoters, 160 passives, 150 detractors.**

**Step 1: percentages of all responses.** Promoters 190 ÷ 500 = **38%**. Detractors 150 ÷ 500 = **30%**.

**Step 2: subtract.** NPS = 38 − 30 = **+8**.

**Classic mistakes:**
- Subtracting counts (190 − 150 = 40). Meaningless.
- Dropping passives from the total: 190 ÷ 340 and 150 ÷ 340 give +11.8, an inflated score.
- Treating 7 as a detractor or 8 as a promoter.

**What if?** 60 detractors blame card blocks in two regions. Fix that and move them to passives: detractors fall to 90 (18%), NPS = 38 − 18 = **+20**. Turning 50 passives into promoters instead gives 48 − 30 = **+18**. Both help, but the detractor fix has a clear cause and owner, so do it first.

NPS measures intention, not behaviour: check in your own data that promoters really stay.

cards.question: A bank receives 80 NPS responses: 36 promoters, 24 passives and 20 detractors. What is its NPS?
cards.explanation: Promoters 36 ÷ 80 = 45%; detractors 20 ÷ 80 = 25%; NPS = 45 − 25 = +20. +16 subtracts counts, +45 is the promoter share alone, and +28.6 wrongly removes passives from the total.

cards.front: Company X: 60% promoters, 20% detractors. Company Y: 45% and 5%.
cards.back: Both score +40, but X has four times the detractor share to deal with. Always look at the distribution, not just the score.

cards.front: 400 responses: 140 promoters, 120 passives, 140 detractors. 40 detractors become passives.
cards.back: NPS goes from 35 − 35 = 0 to 35 − 25 = +10, without creating a single new promoter.

cards.front: Can NPS be negative?
cards.back: Yes. 32% promoters and 35% detractors gives 32 − 35 = −3. More detractors than promoters means a negative score.

cards.front: With 50 responses, one detractor becomes a promoter.
cards.back: NPS moves 4 points: detractors fall 2% and promoters rise 2%. In general, 2 ÷ responses × 100. With 25 responses, it's 8 points.

cards.front: Our NPS beats a global hotel benchmark!
cards.back: Meaningless. Benchmarks vary by industry and country, and some cultures rarely give a 10. Compare with your own trend and rivals measured the same way.

cards.front: Where is most of NPS's value?
cards.back: In the follow-up: "What is the main reason for your score?" The number says where; the comment says why.

cards.title: CSAT and CES: satisfaction and ease
cards.body:
**CSAT** asks how satisfied the customer was with an interaction, usually on a 1–5 scale. Always state which method you report:
- **Top-two-box:** (number of 4s and 5s ÷ all responses) × 100. Used in this course unless stated.
- **Average:** the mean score, e.g. 4.1 out of 5.

The two can disagree: half 5s and half 3s averages 4.0 but is only 50% top-two-box; all 4s also averages 4.0 but is 100%.

**CES** measures how easy it was. High effort predicts disloyalty more reliably than delight predicts loyalty. A common format: "*The bank made it easy to handle my issue*", 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). Report the **average** (higher = easier) or the **% agreeing (5, 6 or 7)**.

Older versions ask "How much effort did you put in?" on 1–5, where **lower is better**. So always state the scale and direction, and **never compare scores from different scales.**

**Where:** CES after problem-solving; CSAT for transactions and coaching; NPS for relationships.

cards.title: Real case: the effort research
cards.caption: In 2010 researchers at CEB (now part of Gartner) published "Stop Trying to Delight Your Customers" in Harvard Business Review. The team expanded the work in the 2013 book The Effortless Experience.

items.label: Customers studied
items.detail: People who had dealt with service teams by phone or through self-service channels.

items.label: Key finding
items.detail: Exceeding expectations added little loyalty; reducing the effort customers had to make did far more.

items.label: After high-effort service
items.detail: Share of customers who became more disloyal, as reported in The Effortless Experience.

items.label: After low-effort service
items.detail: Share who became more disloyal after an easy experience, in the same research.

items.label: What it popularised
items.detail: The Customer Effort Score, now used alongside NPS and CSAT.

cards.title: Polite agents, painful process
cards.body:
A health insurer's helpline collects 400 responses in one week.

**CSAT (1–5):** 5 = 180, 4 = 120, 3 = 50, 2 = 30, 1 = 20.
- Top-two-box = (180 + 120) ÷ 400 = **75%**.
- Average = (900 + 480 + 150 + 60 + 20) ÷ 400 = 1,610 ÷ 400 ≈ **4.03**.

**CES (1–7, higher = easier):** 7 = 100, 6 = 120, 5 = 60, 4 = 40, 3 = 40, 2 = 20, 1 = 20.
- Average = (700 + 720 + 300 + 160 + 120 + 40 + 20) ÷ 400 = 2,060 ÷ 400 = **5.15**.
- % agree (5–7) = 280 ÷ 400 = **70%**.

One caller in five (80) rated ease at 3 or below. Filtered by reason, they clustered on **hospital pre-authorisation calls**, where callers were bounced between the helpline and the medical team. Agents still scored well on courtesy. The fix belonged to the pre-authorisation process, not to agent coaching.

cards.title: Effort versus satisfaction
cards.caption: Plot each journey or call reason. The top-right box is the trap Orvana Bank fell into: lovely staff, exhausting process.

items.label: Easy and pleasing
items.detail: Low effort, high satisfaction. Protect it and learn from it.

items.label: Charming but tiring
items.detail: High effort, high satisfaction. Courteous staff mask a broken process: hidden churn risk.

items.label: Easy but disappointing
items.detail: Low effort, low satisfaction. Check the outcome, price or product itself.

items.label: Fix first
items.detail: High effort, low satisfaction. Churn hotspot: start root-cause work here.

cards.question: A 7-point CES question ("Orvana Bank made it easy to handle my request", 7 = strongly agree) gets 200 responses: 7 = 60, 6 = 60, 5 = 40, 4 = 20, 3 = 20. Which pair of results is correct?
options: Average 5.0; 80% agree
Average 5.6; 60% agree
Average 5.6; 80% agree
Average 4.0; 70% agree
cards.explanation: Average = (420 + 360 + 200 + 80 + 60) ÷ 200 = 1,120 ÷ 200 = 5.6. Agree = scores 5–7 = (60 + 60 + 40) ÷ 200 = 80%. 60% would count only 6s and 7s. On this scale higher means easier, so this is a fairly good result.

cards.title: The 88% question
cards.setting: Omar's desk, later that afternoon. He has pulled ten 'resolved' calls at random.

lines.text: Seven of these ten customers called back within a week about the same thing. My agents ticked 'resolved' because their bonus scorecard counts it.
Agent-reported FCR says 88%. The repeat-contact method says about 70%, where it always was.
I wanted the number to be true. Warden, how should we be counting this?
Count issues, not calls. And let the customer's behaviour decide what 'resolved' means.

cards.title: First-contact resolution, counted honestly
cards.body:
**FCR = issues resolved at first contact ÷ total issues × 100.**

**Count issues, not calls.** A customer who calls three times about one problem is one issue with two repeat contacts.

**Defining 'resolved':**
- **Repeat-contact method:** resolved if the customer doesn't contact you again about the same issue within a set window, often 7 days. The most reliable.
- **Customer-reported:** "Was your issue resolved?" Useful, but only covers respondents.
- **Agent-reported:** a tick box. Easy, and easily inflated.

**Example:** 10,000 calls about 4,000 issues; 1,000 issues saw a repeat contact within 7 days. FCR = 3,000 ÷ 4,000 = **75%** (not 3,000 ÷ 10,000 = 30%).

**Pair metrics so one checks another:** average handling time with FCR (rushed calls come back); complaint closure time with reopened complaints; sales with mis-selling complaints.

cards.title: Match the metric to what it measures
cards.prompt: Each metric answers a different question. Match them up.

pairs.right: How likely customers are to recommend you: a loyalty indicator
How satisfied a customer was with a specific interaction or product
How easy it was for the customer to get their issue handled
Share of issues resolved without the customer needing to come back
Time spent per contact: efficiency and staffing, not quality
Whether complaints marked closed were really fixed

cards.question: In a month, a contact centre records 9,000 contacts relating to 3,600 unique issues. For 900 of those issues, the customer contacted again about the same issue within 7 days. What is FCR using the repeat-contact method?
cards.explanation: Issues resolved first time = 3,600 − 900 = 2,700, and 2,700 ÷ 3,600 = 75%. 30% divides by contacts instead of issues, 25% is the repeat-issue rate, and 40% is issues ÷ contacts, which measures nothing useful.

cards.title: Gaming, bias or sound practice?
cards.prompt: Wanjiru is auditing how scores are collected across Orvana Bank. Sort each practice.

items.text: "If you give me a 10, it really helps my evaluation."
Manager asks a detractor, "Would you now revise your score?"
Agents choose which calls receive the survey
Branch-experience survey sent only by in-app notification
Complaints marked resolved before the customer agrees
Surveys triggered automatically from the core system for every eligible transaction
League table shows CSAT beside response rate and complaint rate
Manager calls a detractor to understand, fix and thank them

cards.title: The branch with perfect scores
cards.situation: Deira branch, Dubai: 98% top-two-box CSAT for three months (network average 82%). Wanjiru finds its response rate is 4% against 15% elsewhere, most responses come from customers whose mobile numbers were updated at the branch that day, complaints from its customers to the central line rose 30%, and a mystery shopper was told, "Sir, please rate us 5." Lukas wants to pay the bonus on Friday. What do you advise?

choices.text: Pay the bonus; 98% for three months can't be luck
choices.outcome: You reward survey steering, and other branches learn the trick by next quarter. Scores rise everywhere while complaints keep climbing.

choices.text: Hold the bonus, trigger surveys automatically to numbers already on record, show response and complaint rates beside CSAT, and coach the manager
choices.outcome: Under the new method the branch scores 80%, close to average. The manager is coached, not sacked, because the incentive invited the behaviour, and the bonus moves to a balanced scorecard.

choices.text: Dismiss the branch manager publicly as a warning
choices.outcome: Fear spreads, but the incentive design that encouraged gaming is unchanged. People get better at hiding it rather than stopping.

choices.text: Wait another quarter and see if the score holds
choices.outcome: Better than celebrating, but the warning signs are already clear. Another quarter of biased data and rising complaints helps nobody.

cards.title: Spot gaming and small-sample noise
cards.body:
**Goodhart's law:** when a measure becomes a target, people hit the target without improving reality.

**Warning signs:** scores jump while complaints, repeat contacts or churn don't; uniform 10s or 5s; one unit's response rate far below others; agent-reported resolution far above customer-reported.

**Prevent it:** automatic random or complete sampling, paired metrics, scores used for learning first, audits.

**Small samples swing.** With 50 responses, one detractor turning promoter shifts NPS 4 points; a 30-response branch can move 10 points by chance. Check counts and response rates, compare like with like, use rolling trends.

cards.title: Real case: Wells Fargo and the cost of targets
cards.body:
In 2016 US regulators and the Los Angeles City Attorney fined Wells Fargo a total of about **USD 185m**. They found that, under intense sales targets, employees had opened deposit and credit-card accounts that customers had not authorised. The bank's own review at the time estimated about **2 million** such accounts, and it said about **5,300 employees** had been dismissed over several years for related misconduct.

- The goals rewarded the number of products sold, so some staff hit the number instead of serving the customer.
- The bank announced it would end product-sales goals for its retail branch staff.
- In 2020 it agreed to pay about **USD 3bn** to resolve related criminal and civil investigations.

**Lesson for you:** this is Goodhart's law at scale. Pair every sales or score target with a measure that would reveal harm, such as complaints about products customers never asked for, and change incentives that reward the wrong behaviour.

cards.title: Closing the loop, inner and outer
cards.caption: Steps 1–3 are the inner loop with one customer. Steps 4–6 are the outer loop that removes causes across the organisation, fed by the inner loop.

items.label: 1. Alert a named owner
items.detail: A low score or serious comment goes straight to the responsible team lead or branch manager.

items.label: 2. Call within two days
items.detail: Understand, fix what you can and thank them. Never argue about the score or ask them to change it.

items.label: 3. Record the root cause
items.detail: Log what happened and why, in a consistent code.

items.label: 4. Group the causes
items.detail: Pareto across many calls, complaints and surveys to find the biggest patterns.

items.label: 5. Cross-functional owner
items.detail: Each major cause gets an owner, an action plan and a deadline, reviewed in a senior CX forum.

items.label: 6. Tell customers
items.detail: "You told us the reminders were missing; we've fixed it." Trust in feedback grows.

cards.question: Wanjiru's alert flags Rosa's score of 3, and you call her. Which aim fits closing the inner loop?
options: Explain why her score was unfair, then ask her to revise it
Understand her experience, fix what you can, thank her and record the root cause
Group her comment with others and assign a cross-functional owner
Send her the same survey again next week to see if the score has improved
cards.explanation: The inner loop is about the individual: understand, fix, thank, record. Asking for a better score corrupts the data. Grouping causes and assigning owners is outer-loop work, and re-surveying her is not closing anything.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Observatory of Signals
items: NPS = % promoters (9–10) − % detractors (0–6); passives stay in the total; range −100 to +100. Look at the distribution, not just the score.
Top-two-box CSAT = share of 4s and 5s; average CSAT is the mean. Always say which you report.
CES measures ease: state the scale and direction, and never compare scores from different scales.
FCR counts issues, not calls; the repeat-contact method beats agent tick boxes. Pair AHT with FCR and closure time with reopened complaints.
Small samples swing: with n responses one switch moves NPS by 2 ÷ n × 100 points. Read trends, not single months.
Close the inner loop with each customer and the outer loop on root causes; automate surveys to prevent gaming.

cards.prompt: Which CX metric does your team watch most closely? How exactly is it calculated, how many responses sit behind it, and how could someone improve the number without improving the customer's experience?

quiz.question: A retailer receives 200 NPS responses: 110 scored 9–10, 50 scored 7–8 and 40 scored 0–6. What is the NPS?
quiz.explanation: Promoters 110 ÷ 200 = 55%; detractors 40 ÷ 200 = 20%; NPS = 55 − 20 = +35. +70 subtracts counts; +55 is the promoter share alone; +46.7 excludes passives from the denominator.

quiz.question: A 5-point CSAT survey of 400 customers gives: 5 = 180, 4 = 120, 3 = 50, 2 = 30, 1 = 20. Which pair of results is correct?
options: Top-two-box CSAT 87.5%; average about 4.03
Top-two-box CSAT 45%; average 4.5
Top-two-box CSAT 75%; average about 4.03
Top-two-box CSAT 75%; average 3.0
quiz.explanation: Top-two-box = (180 + 120) ÷ 400 = 75%. Average = (900 + 480 + 150 + 60 + 20) ÷ 400 = 1,610 ÷ 400 ≈ 4.03. 87.5% wrongly includes the 3s; 45% counts only the 5s; 3.0 is the scale midpoint, not the average.

quiz.question: A bank uses a 7-point CES question ("The bank made it easy to handle my request", 1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree). From 100 responses: 7 = 30, 6 = 40, 5 = 20, 4 = 5, 3 = 5. What is the average CES?
quiz.explanation: (7×30 + 6×40 + 5×20 + 4×5 + 3×5) ÷ 100 = (210 + 240 + 100 + 20 + 15) ÷ 100 = 585 ÷ 100 = 5.85. On this scale higher means easier, so this is a fairly positive result. 90% of respondents agreed (scores 5–7).

quiz.question: In one month, a contact centre handles 10,000 calls relating to 4,000 unique customer issues. For 3,000 of those issues the customer did not contact again about the same issue within 7 days. Using the repeat-contact method, what is FCR?
quiz.explanation: FCR counts issues, not calls: 3,000 resolved at first contact ÷ 4,000 issues = 75%. 30% divides by total calls (3,000 ÷ 10,000); 40% is issues ÷ calls, which is not a resolution measure.

quiz.question: A branch's quarterly NPS rose from +20 to +24. Each quarter is based on about 50 responses. The area manager wants to give the branch an award for improvement. What is the best advice?
options: Treat it as normal variation: with 50 responses one customer can move NPS by 4 points
Approve the award, since a four-point rise in NPS within one quarter is a significant improvement
Reduce the branch's survey sample to avoid confusion
Convert the NPS to CSAT, which is more stable
quiz.explanation: With 50 responses, one detractor becoming a promoter changes NPS by 4 points (2 ÷ 50 × 100). A four-point move is well within chance variation. Smaller samples make it worse, and NPS cannot simply be converted to CSAT.

quiz.question: Company X has 60% promoters and 20% detractors. Company Y has 45% promoters and 5% detractors. Which statement is correct?
options: X has the higher NPS because it has more promoters
Y has the higher NPS because it has fewer detractors
Both have NPS +40, but X has four times the detractor share to address
NPS cannot be calculated without first knowing the exact share of passives in each company
quiz.explanation: X: 60 − 20 = +40. Y: 45 − 5 = +40. Equal scores can hide very different distributions; X has four times the detractor share. Passives are simply the remainder (20% and 50%) and are not needed for the calculation.

quiz.question: A telecom wants to know whether the redesign of its SIM replacement process made it easier for customers. Which measure is most directly suited?
options: A twice-yearly relationship NPS survey
A transactional CES question asked soon after a SIM replacement
The number of new SIM sales
Average handling time in the call centre
quiz.explanation: Ease of a specific process is best measured by a transactional effort question asked right after the experience. Relationship NPS is too broad and slow; SIM sales and AHT do not measure ease for the customer.

quiz.question: At the end of a call, an agent says: "You will receive a short survey; if you give me 10, it really helps my evaluation." What is the main problem?
options: The agent should mention the survey only in English
The agent should ask for a 9 rather than a 10, so that the request sounds more realistic
Surveys should never be mentioned to customers
It is survey begging, which inflates scores and makes the data unreliable
quiz.explanation: Asking for a specific score biases responses and is a classic form of metric gaming. Telling customers a survey is coming can be acceptable; asking for a particular score is not, whatever the number.

quiz.question: Which activity is part of closing the outer loop rather than the inner loop?
options: Grouping root causes from detractor calls and assigning a cross-functional owner
Calling a detractor within two working days to understand the issue and agree a fix
Waiving a fee for a customer who complained
Thanking a customer for their feedback by SMS
quiz.explanation: The outer loop deals with patterns and root causes across many customers, assigning owners and actions. Calling a detractor, fixing their issue and thanking them are inner-loop activities with individual customers.

quiz.question: A contact centre manager sets a strict target to cut average handling time by 20%. Which companion metric would best reveal whether this is harming customers?
options: Number of agents on shift
Call abandonment rate
Repeat contacts on the same issue within 7 days (FCR)
Number of calls answered per hour
quiz.explanation: If agents rush to cut handling time, issues go unresolved and customers call back. FCR/repeat contact catches that directly. Calls per hour moves with AHT and would hide the harm; abandonment and staffing do not show resolution quality.

sessions.title: Designing and Leading a CX Culture
sessions.summary: Turn CX from a project into a way of working: set service standards, improve employee experience, empower staff within guardrails, manage complaints to the standard regulators expect, improve continuously and build a CX strategy and business case leaders will fund.
objectives: Write service standards that are specific, observable and grounded in customer needs
Explain the link between employee experience, empowerment and customer experience
Describe international complaint-handling principles and escalation routes in regulated sectors in several countries
Apply continuous improvement cycles and pilots to CX changes
Build a CX strategy and a quantified business case

cards.title: Two weeks to the board
cards.setting: The Citadel: Orvana Bank's regional boardroom in Dubai, empty for now. Priya has gathered the whole team around the Lantern Board.

lines.text: The board meets in two weeks. I'll back a CX programme, but only with a case I can defend line by line. No balloons, no 'customer week'.
And my agents escalate about 3,000 small fee waivers a month. Supervisors approve 97% of them, after a 30-minute wait. Customers hate it. So do we.
Omar called me at 11:30, before the time he promised. And now I get a text in Portuguese when my pension arrives. Small things, but nobody did them in 22 years.
Her lantern's brighter. But one fix for one journey won't hold the whole network. Thousands are still flickering.
Final stage, Warden. You've mended one promise. Now build a culture that keeps every lantern lit, and make Lukas proud to fund it.

scenes.heading: Promises are not behaviour
scenes.narration: "We put customers first" means little to a teller at three o'clock on salary day. Service standards turn the brand promise into concrete behaviours staff can deliver and managers can check.

scenes.heading: Specific and observable
scenes.narration: "Be friendly" can't be checked. "Greet every customer within 30 seconds of reaching the counter" can. Good standards come from what customers value at each moment of truth.

scenes.heading: Realistic, and backed backstage
scenes.narration: A standard the system can't deliver teaches staff to ignore all standards. If dispatch can't produce two-hour delivery windows, fix dispatch first, or change the standard.

scenes.heading: Few and owned
scenes.narration: Five to ten core standards per channel get remembered; fifty don't. Each needs a way to be checked: mystery shopping, call review, system data or customer feedback.

scenes.heading: Standards, not scripts
scenes.narration: Standards define what must happen and leave room for how. Rigid word-for-word scripts sound robotic. Keep exact wording only where it is required, such as regulatory disclosures and security checks.

cards.title: Standard or wish?
cards.prompt: Which of these could guide behaviour tomorrow, and which need rewriting?

items.text: Confirm the next step, timeline and reference number at the end of every interaction
Reply to WhatsApp messages within 15 minutes during service hours
Quote all fees and charges before the customer signs
Greet every customer within 30 seconds of reaching the counter
Always delight our valued customers
Be friendly and professional at all times
Read this 120-word opening word for word on every call
Two-hour delivery window by SMS, when dispatch cannot yet plan two-hour windows

cards.question: A private hospital sets a standard: "Give inpatient families a written cost estimate within 24 hours of admission." Its billing system currently needs three days to produce an estimate. What must happen for the standard to work?
options: Train front-desk staff to apologise when estimates are late
Change the billing process so estimates can actually be produced within 24 hours
Drop all written standards and rely on staff goodwill
Measure the standard monthly and discipline staff who miss it
cards.explanation: A standard depends on the backstage process behind it. Without a billing change it is impossible, and staff learn to ignore standards. Apologies and discipline punish people for a system limit.

cards.title: The service-profit chain
cards.caption: A well-known management model linking employee experience to customer loyalty and profit. Research supports the link, though its strength varies by industry.

items.label: Supported employees
items.detail: Working tools, sensible workload, fair targets, support after hard calls, recognition, a voice.

items.label: Better service
items.detail: Capable, empowered staff resolve issues faster and with more care.

items.label: Customer loyalty
items.detail: Customers stay, buy more and recommend.

items.label: Growth and profit
items.detail: Retention, referrals and lower cost to serve fund the next improvements.

cards.title: Employee experience drives customer experience
cards.body:
Customers can only experience what employees are able to deliver.

- **Tools that work.** Slow systems and five logins frustrate staff and customers alike.
- **Workload planned for known peaks:** month-start salaries and pensions, holiday seasons.
- **Targets that don't fight service.** A cross-sell quota on every walk-in pushes staff into behaviour they know customers dislike. That is an incentive problem, not a sales-skills problem.
- **Support after hard interactions:** short breaks and supervisor debriefs after abusive calls.
- **Recognition** for real customer outcomes, and **being heard** on broken processes.

Contact centres in many countries struggle with staff turnover. A centre with 60% annual attrition, slow systems and chaotic month-end rosters will have weak FCR however fast it hires. Fixing tools, rosters and support improves both experiences. Track engagement or eNPS beside customer metrics.

cards.title: The waiver that backfired
cards.setting: Contact centre break room, Toronto. Omar is still upset about something he heard from the Singapore team last week.

lines.text: A Singapore officer, Mei Lin, gave an SGD 50 goodwill waiver, well within her authority, to a customer whose card was wrongly blocked abroad.
Her manager criticised her in front of the whole branch: 'I would have given less.' Now she escalates every single waiver. Customers wait. She hates it.
From a risk point of view, I like approvals. They feel safe.
Do they? 97% of escalated waivers get approved. The approval adds 30 minutes of delay and almost no control.
Empowerment without safety is a trap, Lukas. Warden, design guardrails that let Mei Lin help, and let you sleep at night.

cards.title: Empowerment within guardrails
cards.caption: Empowerment means authority, information and confidence to fix problems without needless escalation. Read from the top: the hard limits first, the foundation last.

items.label: Non-negotiables
items.detail: KYC and identity checks, AML, credit decisions and data privacy are never frontline discretion.

items.label: Clear decision rights
items.detail: For example: agents waive up to USD 25, branch managers up to USD 150, above that the regional head.

items.label: Principles for judgement
items.detail: Restore the customer to where they would have been; add a gesture when inconvenience was significant.

items.label: Logging and review
items.detail: Reason codes for every discretionary action; patterns reviewed for consistency and misuse.

items.label: Information and skills
items.detail: Access to customer history and case status; training in judgement using real cases.

items.label: Psychological safety
items.detail: Good-faith decisions within authority are supported. Coach privately; never shame publicly.

cards.title: Real case: Ritz-Carlton's USD 2,000 rule
cards.body:
Luxury hotel group Ritz-Carlton is widely cited for one empowerment rule: each employee may spend up to **USD 2,000 per guest** to put a problem right, without first asking a manager. The company has described the rule publicly for many years.

- The limit is generous, and company leaders have said the full amount is rarely needed. Its main effect is **speed and confidence**: staff act on the spot instead of escalating.
- It sits inside written service standards (the company's "Gold Standards") and a short daily team meeting where real guest stories are shared, so judgement is trained rather than left to chance.

**Lesson for you:** your limits will differ, but the design is the same: clear decision rights, principles for judgement, logging and review, and managers who back good-faith decisions.

cards.title: 3,000 waivers a month
cards.situation: Agents escalate about 3,000 requests a month to waive SMS-alert and late fees below USD 5. Supervisors approve 97% of them, after a 30-minute average delay. Customers call back to chase. Lukas worries about losing control. What do you recommend?

choices.text: Hire two more supervisors so approvals come faster
choices.outcome: Delays shrink a little and costs rise, but you are still paying people to approve what is almost always approved.

choices.text: Let agents waive these fees up to a set limit, with reason codes and a monthly report that flags unusual patterns
choices.outcome: Most waivers are now granted on the first call. Repeat contacts fall, supervisors focus on complex cases, and the report catches one agent who misread the codes, who is retrained. Lukas gets control through data, not delay.

choices.text: Keep approvals but set supervisors a five-minute response target
choices.outcome: Faster than before, so customers suffer less. But the step still adds little control, and supervisors are now chasing a stopwatch instead of hard cases.

choices.text: Ask customers to email their waiver requests to a central team
choices.outcome: You have moved the effort onto the customer and added days. Complaints rise and the original problem is untouched.

cards.title: Complaints in regulated sectors
cards.body:
In banking, insurance and telecoms, regulators treat poor complaint handling as a **conduct issue**. Two international reference points: the **G20/OECD principles on financial consumer protection**, where complaint handling and redress is a core principle, and **ISO 10002**, a guideline for complaint handling in any organisation.

**Expectations common across countries:**
- A dedicated complaint function with senior oversight, and channels that are easy to find.
- Prompt acknowledgement with a **reference number**, resolution within set timelines, and updates.
- A **clear, reasoned final reply** that explains how to escalate.
- **Analysis**: root causes, trends by product and channel, repeat complaints and outcomes, reported to senior management and the board, plus a check on who else is affected.
- Never penalise a customer for complaining.

Timelines and ombudsman rules differ by country and change, so **always check the rules where you work.**

cards.title: The escalation ladder for a bank complaint
cards.caption: Who handles what varies. The UK and Australian schemes cover banking and insurance; India and Pakistan have separate insurance ombudsmen. Telecom disputes usually go to the operator first, then a regulator or approved scheme. Check the rules where you work.

items.label: Complain to the bank
items.detail: In any channel: branch, helpline, chat, app, website.

items.label: Get a reference number
items.detail: Logged in one system, so every channel can see it.

items.label: Investigation within timelines
items.detail: Check the transactions, not just the fee schedule; keep the customer informed.

items.label: Final reasoned reply
items.detail: Plain language, the customer's preferred language, and the escalation options.

items.label: Independent ombudsman
items.detail: Free for consumers. E.g. UK: Financial Ombudsman Service (after a final reply or 8 weeks). Australia: AFCA. India: RBI Ombudsman. Pakistan: Banking Mohtasib.

cards.title: Where should this complaint go next?
cards.prompt: Match each situation to the most appropriate next step.

pairs.left: UK bank customer unhappy with the bank's final response
pairs.right: The Financial Ombudsman Service, free for consumers

pairs.left: Australian customer unhappy with an insurer's final response
pairs.right: The Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA)

pairs.left: Pakistani bank customer unhappy with the bank's final reply
pairs.right: The Banking Mohtasib Pakistan, an independent banking ombudsman

pairs.left: Customer upset about a bank fee who hasn't told the bank yet
pairs.right: The bank's own complaint channel first, with a reference number

pairs.left: Three complaints in a week about the same unexplained card fee
pairs.right: Check for a systemic error and correct every affected account

cards.title: Real case: the UK's PPI complaints wave
cards.body:
Payment protection insurance (PPI) was sold with loans, credit cards and mortgages in the UK for many years. Regulators found widespread mis-selling: many customers did not know they had bought it, did not need it or could never have claimed on it.

- Complaints ran into the millions, and PPI became the largest single type of case at the Financial Ombudsman Service.
- In **2015** the Financial Conduct Authority fined Lloyds Banking Group about **GBP 117m** for failing to handle PPI complaints fairly in 2012–13.
- The FCA set a final deadline for PPI complaints of **29 August 2019**. Firms paid out about **GBP 38bn** in redress in total.

**Lesson for you:** sales incentives create complaints later, and complaint handling is itself regulated. Regulators check that complaints are investigated fairly, that root causes are fixed, and that other affected customers are put right too.

cards.title: Plan, Do, Check, Act
cards.caption: Improvement as a routine, not a campaign. Many things change at once in a business, so a control group separates your effect from the season.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Define the problem with data, find the root cause and write a hypothesis: 'A dormancy-warning SMS will cut card-block calls by a third.'

items.label: Do
items.detail: Test small: a few branches, one region or a share of customers.

items.label: Check
items.detail: Compare with a control group that didn't get the change, over long enough to trust.

items.label: Act
items.detail: Scale what works, adjust what partly works, stop what doesn't. Then plan the next cycle.

cards.question: Orvana Bank pilots dormancy-warning SMS in eight branches. Card-block calls there fall 30% over two months. In eight similar control branches without the SMS, they fall 18% over the same period because of a seasonal dip. What is the best estimate of the SMS's effect?
options: A 30% reduction
About 12 points, the difference from the control branches
A 48% reduction, adding both falls together
No effect, because the control branches also improved
cards.explanation: The control branches show that about 18 points of the fall would have happened anyway. The extra 12 points is the best estimate of the SMS's effect, to be confirmed with more data. Claiming 30% ignores the control; saying zero ignores the extra gain.

cards.title: CX strategy in four questions
cards.body:
1. **What experience do we want to be known for?** Specific and tied to target customers, e.g. "the easiest bank for pensioners and small traders".
2. **Which journeys matter most?** Pick a handful using **value at stake (customers, revenue, risk) combined with today's pain**. Ease of fixing helps you sequence quick wins; it shouldn't set the strategy alone.
3. **How will we organise?** A senior CX forum, named cross-functional journey owners, a voice-of-the-customer programme and a measurement framework.
4. **How will we fund and sequence it?** Quick wins for credibility, plus structural fixes to processes, systems and policies.

**New CX head with 90 days?** Choose two or three journeys from evidence, set up the forum with owners, and deliver measured quick wins. Not a technology purchase first, not bonuses tied to an untested NPS, and not a branding week with courtesy training.

cards.title: Your business case for Lukas
cards.caption: Failure demand: calls caused by things going wrong. Own data, a controlled pilot, a conservative estimate, complete costs, and no double-counting.

items.label: Card-block calls a year
items.detail: 1.5 million calls × 20% about dormancy and card blocks.

items.label: Calls avoided (conservative)
items.detail: The pilot cut 40% against control; you plan on 30%.

items.label: Net annual saving
items.detail: 90,000 × USD 4 per call = USD 360,000, minus USD 60,000 a year to run the SMS service.

items.label: Payback on USD 450,000
items.detail: One-off cost ÷ net annual saving: 450,000 ÷ 300,000. Low case (20%) = 2.5 years; high (40%) ≈ 1.1 years.

cards.title: Calculate the payback
cards.prompt: Put the steps of a failure-demand payback calculation in the right order.
steps: Work out the annual calls of this type: total calls × share for this reason
Apply the expected reduction to find the calls avoided
Multiply calls avoided by the cost per call to get gross annual savings
Subtract annual running costs to get net annual savings
Divide the one-off cost by net annual savings to get payback in years

cards.question: A contact centre takes 1,000,000 calls a year; 20% ask "where is my card?". A tracking feature should cut those calls by 50%. Cost per call is USD 5. The feature costs USD 750,000 one-off plus USD 100,000 a year to run. What is the approximate payback?
options: About 1.5 years
About 6 months
About 1.9 years
About 7.5 years
cards.explanation: 200,000 card calls × 50% = 100,000 avoided × USD 5 = USD 500,000 a year. Net of running costs: 500,000 − 100,000 = USD 400,000. Payback = 750,000 ÷ 400,000 ≈ 1.9 years. 1.5 years ignores the running cost; 6 months inverts the ratio; 7.5 years divides by the running cost alone.

cards.title: Credible cases, not CX theatre
cards.body:
**Finance trusts cases that:** use your own data; label assumptions and keep them conservative; show low, expected and high ranges; include every cost (technology, training, process change, staff time); and **never double-count**. A call saved can't appear as a cost saving and again as a retention gain for the same customers.

**Signs of CX theatre:** a 'customer week' with balloons but no process changes; dashboards reviewed monthly with no decisions recorded; a CX team with no authority over any journey; awards for scores customers' behaviour doesn't confirm.

**The test:** what changed for customers this quarter, and how do we know?

cards.title: The lanterns of Orvana
cards.setting: Board meeting, two weeks later. Then, that evening, the Lantern Board.

lines.text: Own data, a controlled pilot, a conservative range, all costs in, nothing counted twice. I've read worse cases from consultants. The board approves.
And from Monday my agents can waive small fees themselves, with reason codes. Mei Lin has already stopped escalating.
Wanjiru's survey asked again. I gave a 9. I told my neighbour to open her pension account here, and my son can keep his bank.
Look: a whole district of lanterns brighter this quarter. Pension customers' detractor share is down by a third.
You saw, you listened, you mended and you measured. Now one gate remains, Warden: the final exam. Pass it, and Orvana's lanterns are in your care.

cards.title: Take-aways from the Citadel of Lanterns
items: Service standards are few, specific, observable, realistic and needs-based, backed by backstage processes; keep exact scripts for disclosures and security only.
Employee experience drives customer experience: tools, planned workload, fair targets, support after hard calls and recognition all matter.
Empower staff with decision rights, logging, information and psychological safety, inside non-negotiable regulatory guardrails.
Regulated complaints: references, timelines, reasoned replies, escalation options, root causes and systemic checks. Ombudsmen such as the UK FOS, AFCA and the Banking Mohtasib are external routes.
Improve with PDCA and control groups; the effect is the difference from the control.
A credible business case: own data, conservative ranges, complete costs, payback = one-off cost ÷ net annual savings, and no double-counting.

cards.prompt: If you had to present one CX improvement to your leadership next month, which journey would you choose, what value sources would you quantify, and what pilot with a control group would prove it works?

quiz.question: Which of the following is the best-written service standard?
options: Always provide excellent and friendly service
Confirm the next step, timeline and reference number at the end of every customer interaction
Make every customer feel like family
Do your best to resolve complaints quickly
quiz.explanation: Option B is specific, observable and measurable, and links to what customers value. The others express good intentions but cannot be consistently checked or coached.

quiz.question: A retailer introduces a standard: "All home-delivery customers receive a two-hour delivery window by SMS the evening before." After two months, the standard is met for only 40% of deliveries, and staff have started ignoring it. What is the most likely cause?
options: Customers do not want delivery windows
The standard is not specific enough for staff to know exactly what is expected of them
Staff were not told about the standard
Backstage dispatch cannot yet produce two-hour windows reliably
quiz.explanation: The standard is specific and clearly communicated, but staff cannot meet it without a supporting process. Standards that the system cannot deliver teach staff to ignore standards. Fix the backstage capability or adjust the standard.

quiz.question: Which statement best reflects the service-profit chain idea?
options: Profit should be maximised first, so that the company can afford to pay employees more
Customer loyalty is determined mainly by price
Supported, capable employees give better service, which builds loyalty and profit
Employee satisfaction and customer satisfaction are unrelated
quiz.explanation: The model links internal service quality and employee experience to service value, loyalty and profit. It does not claim price is the main driver, and it explicitly connects employee and customer outcomes.

quiz.question: Data shows that agents escalate around 3,000 requests a month to waive SMS-alert charges below USD 5, and supervisors approve 97% of them, usually after a 30-minute delay. What is the best leadership action?
options: Let agents waive charges up to a limit, with reason codes and monitoring
Stop all waivers to remove the workload
Hire additional supervisors so that each approval takes five minutes rather than thirty
Ask customers to submit waiver requests in writing
quiz.explanation: When nearly all escalations are approved, the approval step adds delay and cost but little control. Empowerment with limits, reason codes and monitoring keeps risk managed while speeding resolution. The other options add cost or effort.

quiz.question: A branch officer gave a USD 40 goodwill waiver, within her authority, to a customer whose card was wrongly blocked abroad. Her manager publicly criticises her, saying he would have offered less. What is the likely effect on CX culture?
options: Staff will make more consistent decisions
Staff lose psychological safety and start escalating decisions they are allowed to make
Customers will receive larger waivers in future
There will be no effect on staff, because the waiver was within policy and the customer was retained
quiz.explanation: Empowerment depends on staff trusting that reasonable decisions within their authority will be supported. Public criticism teaches them to escalate everything, which slows recovery. Coaching privately on judgement would have been appropriate.

quiz.question: Under international principles and most national rules, which of the following is generally expected of a bank's complaint-handling process?
options: Complaints may be resolved informally and left unrecorded when the customer seems satisfied with the outcome
Complaints should be accepted only in writing at the branch where the account is held
Customers should be told that the bank's decision is final
Acknowledge with a reference, resolve within set timelines, give reasons and explain escalation options
quiz.explanation: The G20/OECD principles and national rules broadly expect acknowledgement with a reference, timely resolution, reasoned responses and information on further escalation, such as an independent ombudsman. Unrecorded complaints, restricted channels and claims of finality all conflict with these expectations.

quiz.question: A bank's complaint unit notices three complaints in one week about the same unexplained card fee. What should it do beyond resolving the three cases?
options: Wait a few more weeks to see whether more customers complain before starting any investigation
Ask the three customers not to discuss the issue publicly
Check whether a systemic error affects others and correct all affected accounts
Refund the three customers and close the matter
quiz.explanation: Clusters of similar complaints often signal a systemic issue. Fair treatment requires checking for other affected customers and correcting their accounts proactively, not only refunding those who complained. Silencing customers is clearly inappropriate.

quiz.question: A bank pilots a new loan-status SMS in five branches. Calls about loan status from those branches fall 25% over two months. In the same period, calls about loan status from all other branches fall 20% due to a seasonal dip. What is the best estimate of the pilot's effect?
options: A small extra effect of roughly 5 points beyond the seasonal fall, to be confirmed
A 25% reduction, which can be used directly in the business case for a network-wide rollout
No effect at all, so the SMS should be stopped
A 45% reduction, combining both figures
quiz.explanation: The control branches show that most of the fall was seasonal. The SMS adds only about 5 points (strictly, 25% vs 20% is roughly a 6% relative difference). It may still be worthwhile, but needs confirmation over a longer period. Using 25% ignores the control; adding figures is wrong.

quiz.question: A contact centre handles 800,000 calls a year; 25% are "where is my order" calls. A tracking feature is expected to cut those calls by 40%. The cost per call is USD 5 and the feature costs USD 600,000 one-off. What is the approximate payback period on call savings alone?
options: About 6 months
1.5 years
About 3 years
About 8 months
quiz.explanation: 800,000 × 25% = 200,000 calls; × 40% = 80,000 fewer calls; × USD 5 = USD 400,000 a year. Payback = 600,000 ÷ 400,000 = 1.5 years. About 8 months comes from inverting the ratio (400,000 ÷ 600,000 ≈ 0.67 years); 3 years would follow only if calls fell by 20% instead of 40%.

quiz.question: A bank customer in the UK has received the bank's final response to her fee complaint and still considers it unfair. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Open a new complaint at another branch so the timeline starts again
Report the bank to the telecom regulator
Fill in the bank's customer satisfaction survey
Take it to the Financial Ombudsman Service, free of charge
quiz.explanation: In the UK, a customer who is unhappy with a firm's final response (or has had none after 8 weeks) can take the complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service, which is free for consumers. Restarting the complaint delays her, the telecom regulator has no role, and a survey is not an escalation route.

bank.question: A microfinance bank earns an average annual profit of USD 90 per active borrower and retains 70% of borrowers each year. Using the simple estimate CLV ≈ annual profit × (1 ÷ churn), what is the approximate lifetime value of a borrower?
options: USD 63
USD 129
USD 300
USD 270
bank.explanation: Churn = 1 − 0.70 = 0.30, so expected relationship ≈ 1 ÷ 0.30 ≈ 3.33 years. CLV ≈ 90 × 3.33 = USD 300. USD 270 rounds the relationship down to 3 years; USD 129 divides by retention; USD 63 multiplies by retention.

bank.question: A regional bank has 50,000 retail customers, each producing USD 100 annual profit. A CX programme is expected to lift retention from 75% to 80%. Using CLV ≈ annual profit ÷ churn, roughly how much total lifetime value does the improvement add across the base?
options: USD 5 million
USD 25 million
USD 1.25 million
bank.explanation: CLV rises from 100 ÷ 0.25 = 400 to 100 ÷ 0.20 = 500, a gain of USD 100 per customer. × 50,000 customers = USD 5 million. USD 25 million is the new total CLV, not the gain; USD 250,000 applies the 5-point change to one year's profit.

bank.question: At a strategy meeting, a telecom's chief operating officer says: "CX is the contact centre's responsibility; their scores are excellent, so we are fine." Meanwhile complaints about billing errors and network drops are rising. Which reply best reflects CX thinking?
options: Agree, and ask the contact centre to absorb the higher complaint volumes by recruiting more agents
Agree, but add a CSAT survey for billing calls to confirm the scores
Disagree, and move the contact centre under the marketing department
Disagree: billing and the network shape experience, so CX needs shared, top-led ownership
bank.explanation: Experience is created by every function; billing systems and the network are owned outside the contact centre. Good agent scores cannot remove the causes. Extra staff or extra surveys treat symptoms, and moving reporting lines does not create shared ownership.

bank.question: A bank's retention rate is 94%, but only 1.2 products are held per customer, relationship NPS is −15, and most accounts are salary accounts opened through employers. A large employer is considering moving its payroll to a digital bank. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: High retention proves strong loyalty, so losing the employer's payroll would affect few customers
Much of the retention is captive, so the base is exposed if payroll moves
Low product holding shows customers are price-sensitive, so fees should be cut
A negative NPS is normal for banks and can be ignored if retention is high
bank.explanation: High retention combined with low share of wallet and negative NPS signals captive behaviour rather than attitudinal loyalty. When the employer changes payroll bank, many customers may leave with it. Low product holding alone does not prove price sensitivity.

bank.question: A health insurer's data shows that members whose first claim took over 30 days to settle lapse at renewal at 45%, compared with 15% for members whose first claim was settled within 10 days. With budget for one improvement, which should it prioritise?
options: Speeding up and communicating the first-claim journey
A redesigned welcome pack for new members
Discounts at renewal for all members
A new advertising campaign about claim speed
bank.explanation: The first claim is a moment of truth with a clear, large link to lapse behaviour. Fixing it addresses the cause. Renewal discounts cost money without fixing the experience, and advertising claim speed before improving it raises expectations the insurer cannot meet.

bank.question: Hospital discharge takes about four hours. Families report that the worst moment is being called to the billing counter and told, in front of others, about unexpected charges. Which change is likely to improve families' memory of the stay most for the least cost?
options: Reduce discharge time from four hours to three and a half by adding a clerk
Send a satisfaction survey by SMS within one hour of discharge
Share cost updates privately each day and review the final bill privately
Install a television and free tea in the discharge lounge
bank.explanation: The peak-end effect means the humiliating billing surprise (a negative peak that also forms the ending) dominates memory. Removing the surprise and handling the ending privately addresses both. A modest time cut costs more and changes memory less; a survey only measures.

bank.question: An insurer earns USD 60 annual profit per policyholder. Retention improves from 85% to 88%. By roughly how much does the simple CLV estimate per policyholder rise?
options: About USD 12
About USD 180
About USD 20
About USD 100
bank.explanation: CLV moves from 60 ÷ 0.15 = 400 to 60 ÷ 0.12 = 500, an increase of about USD 100. USD 12 applies the 3-point change to 400; USD 20 and USD 180 do not follow from the formula. Note that a three-point retention gain increases CLV by 25%.

bank.question: A new credit card arrives on time and works correctly, but activation requires a 12-minute call with long security questions and two transfers. Many customers rate the experience poorly. Which idea best explains this?
options: Customers only value speed of delivery
High effort produces negative emotion even when the outcome is correct
Customers judge experiences by the average of all steps
The product itself must be poor
bank.explanation: The outcome is fine, but effort (time, repetition, transfers) drives frustration and shapes the memory. Averaging is not how memory works, and nothing suggests the product is poor.

bank.question: Which situation is the clearest example of a moment of decision?
options: A customer's first visit to a newly opened branch
A customer reporting a stolen phone late at night and asking to block the SIM
A customer weighing a rival's offer as her car insurance renewal nears
A customer receiving a monthly account statement
bank.explanation: A renewal with a competing offer is a stay-or-leave point where the accumulated experience turns into a choice. A first visit is a first impression; a stolen phone is a moment of need; a routine statement is low-stakes.

bank.question: A bank's CX lead reviews: courtesy scores for call-centre agents at 92%; complaints about card delivery up 40%; relationship NPS down 9 points; retention flat at 93%, driven by payroll accounts. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Courtesy is masking a journey failure; retention may be captive, so card delivery needs a cross-functional owner
Since retention is flat, the NPS decline is most likely survey noise and does not need action in this financial year
The card complaints show agents are failing to explain delivery times, so the priority is script training
Customers are less loyal in general, so the bank should increase acquisition spending to offset future losses
bank.explanation: The evidence points to a journey problem (card delivery) outside the call centre, with flat retention likely supported by captive payroll customers. A 9-point drop alongside rising complaints is unlikely to be noise; script training treats a symptom; acquisition spend ignores the cause.

bank.question: A digital bank sees that 60% of users who start a personal-loan application in the app abandon it at the income-verification step. Which VoC approach will best explain why?
options: A twice-yearly relationship NPS survey of all customers
Funnel analytics on the step, combined with observed usability sessions with target users
A focus group of senior managers who use the app
Counting app-store reviews that mention loans
bank.explanation: Behavioural data locates the drop-off precisely, and watching real users attempt the step reveals why. A relationship survey is too broad; managers are not representative; review counts show volume but not the cause at that step.

bank.question: A bank wants feedback it can use to coach individual branch teams on service at the counter. Which design is most suitable?
options: A national relationship survey run once a year, with results reported by province and region
A social-listening report on mentions of the bank
Exit interviews with customers who close accounts
A short transactional survey sent automatically after branch visits, linked to the branch
bank.explanation: Coaching needs timely feedback about specific interactions, which transactional surveys linked to the branch provide. Annual relationship surveys are too infrequent and aggregated; social listening and exit interviews cannot be reliably tied to particular teams.

bank.question: A motor insurer currently surveys claimants the day a claim is registered, and scores are high. Complaints about claim delays remain common. What change to survey timing is most appropriate?
options: Survey after settlement, with an optional pulse at registration
Stop surveying claimants because the scores are already high
Survey only the claimants whose claims were approved, since they can comment on the whole process
Move the survey to the renewal date one year later
bank.explanation: At registration nothing has been tested yet, so the survey captures hope rather than experience. Surveying after settlement captures delays and outcomes. Surveying only approved claims biases the sample; waiting a year loses detail.

bank.question: A telecom's marketing team created 11 personas two years ago from internal brainstorming. Product teams say they never use them. What is the best way forward?
options: Add more personal detail, such as hobbies and favourite TV shows, so the personas feel memorable
Replace personas with age and income segments, which are easier to measure
Rebuild a few needs-based personas from research and use them in design reviews
Distribute the existing personas again with a memo asking teams to use them
bank.explanation: Personas fail when they are assumption-based, too numerous and not built into decisions. A few evidence-based, needs-based personas used in design reviews fix all three. More trivia, demographic bands or reminders do not address the causes.

bank.question: A retailer's project team wants to start its journey-mapping workshop by designing the ideal future app experience, since "everyone already knows the current problems". What is the strongest advice?
options: Proceed as planned, because designing the future state is the most valuable part of the work
Ask the app vendor to propose the future state instead
Skip mapping and run an NPS survey first
Map the current state with customer evidence first, so the redesign targets real pain
bank.explanation: Assumed knowledge of current problems is often wrong or incomplete. An evidence-based current-state map shows where effort and emotion actually peak. A vendor proposal or an NPS score alone cannot locate pain points within the journey.

bank.question: An electricity distributor investigates billing complaints using the five whys: bills are wrong → readings are estimated → readers cannot access meters inside locked homes → visits happen during working hours when no one is home → ? Which next answer is the most useful root cause to act on?
options: Customers are rarely at home and should stay in more
There is no way for customers to book a reading visit or submit their own verified reading
Meter readers are lazy and need disciplinary action
Estimated billing is permitted under the regulations, so there is no real problem here to solve
bank.explanation: A useful root cause is systemic, within the company's control and fixable with an owner, such as booking or self-submitted readings. Blaming customers or readers stops the analysis too early, and the permissibility of estimates does not remove the complaints.

bank.question: In a blueprint of branch account opening, documents are scanned at the branch, but the original forms are couriered once a day to central operations, which verifies them before activation. Accounts take three days to activate. Which of these is best described as a wait point?
options: Forms waiting for the daily courier batch before central verification can begin
The teller checking the customer's original passport or ID card
Central operations re-typing form data into the core system
The welcome letter the customer receives
bank.explanation: A wait point is where work or the customer sits idle in a queue or batch. Re-typing data is a fail point (error-prone), the ID check is a frontstage action, and the welcome letter is physical evidence.

bank.question: A card unit's monthly contacts are: PIN reset 3,200; card delivery status 2,600; app login 1,400; fee queries 500; other 300. What share of all contacts do the top two reasons represent?
bank.explanation: Total = 8,000. PIN reset + card delivery = 5,800. 5,800 ÷ 8,000 = 72.5%. 90% is the share of the top three. Pareto analysis shows that fixing these two reasons would address most contact volume.

bank.question: A journey map shows customers are anxious after depositing a cheque because the app shows nothing for a day. The service blueprint reveals that clearing is completed the same day, but the app shows transactions only after an overnight posting batch. What is the most effective fix?
options: Train agents to reassure customers who call about deposited cheques
Speed up the clearing process so that every cheque is cleared before noon on the same day
Add a note on the deposit slip asking customers to be patient
Show the backstage status (received, in clearing, cleared) in the app in near real time
bank.explanation: The blueprint shows the delay is in visibility, not processing. Exposing backstage status removes the anxiety at its source. Faster clearing would not help because the app still updates overnight; reassuring callers and slip notes treat symptoms.

bank.question: In a service blueprint, what does the line of visibility separate?
options: Customer actions from physical evidence
Frontstage actions the customer sees from backstage actions they do not see
Support processes from IT systems
Online channels from offline channels
bank.explanation: The line of visibility divides what the customer can see (frontstage) from what happens out of sight (backstage and support). It is not a channel boundary, and it does not split customer actions from physical evidence.

bank.question: An agent tells a customer: "I can't process your address change without the signed form." Which rewording best applies positive, action-focused language while staying accurate?
options: "Once I have the signed form, I can update it the same day. Shall I send it on WhatsApp?"
"Don't worry, I will update your address now and you can send the signed form whenever convenient."
"Unfortunately, that's the policy and I have no choice."
"You should have brought the form with you."
bank.explanation: Option A leads with what can be done, gives a clear timeline and makes the next step easy, without breaking the rule. Option B promises to bypass a control; C is negative and policy-focused; D blames the customer.

bank.question: A quality reviewer notices an agent spent 35 minutes on a call repeatedly reassuring a customer about a failed transfer, with warm language throughout, but never traced the transfer. The customer called again the next day. What is the most useful coaching point?
options: Empathy should be dropped in favour of a strict script
The agent should have transferred the call to a supervisor at once
Empathy should lead quickly to action; warmth without resolution adds effort
The call was handled well, because the customer was treated warmly and patiently throughout
bank.explanation: Empathy is valuable when it leads the customer into a solution. Here it replaced resolution, causing a repeat contact. Dropping empathy goes too far, an immediate transfer adds effort, and warmth alone did not meet the customer's need.

bank.question: A customer arrives upset about a blocked account. Before the customer finishes speaking, the officer explains the bank's dormancy policy in detail. Which LEARN step has been skipped or rushed?
options: Resolve together
Listen and acknowledge
Notify and follow through
Apologise appropriately
bank.explanation: Listen and acknowledge means letting the customer finish and recognising the feeling before explaining or defending. Jumping to policy skips it and usually escalates frustration. The later steps cannot work well until the customer feels heard.

bank.question: A well-known local businessman insists a relationship officer open an account for his nephew today without the required identity documents, saying, "Do you know who I am? Your regional head is my friend." What is the best response?
options: Open the account and collect documents next week, given his importance
Call the regional head and ask for permission to open the account now and collect documents later
Politely refuse and ask him to leave the branch
Stay courteous, explain the rule cannot be waived, and offer the fastest compliant route
bank.explanation: Identity requirements are non-negotiable, whoever the customer is. Treating him with high courtesy while applying the same rule, and offering the quickest compliant path, protects both the customer relationship and the bank. Asking the regional head to bypass the rule is still a breach.

bank.question: A bank debited a trader's USD 3,000 payment twice. As a result, his cheque to a supplier bounced, he paid a bounce charge and was embarrassed with his supplier. Which recovery is most appropriate?
options: Reverse the duplicate debit and send a standard apology SMS
Reverse the duplicate debit and offer a free cheque book
Reverse it, refund the bounce charge, give a letter admitting the error, apologise and fix the cause
Ask the trader to submit a formal written complaint so the case can be investigated within the usual timeline
bank.explanation: Recovery should restore the customer fully, including knock-on costs, and repair reputational harm, here with a letter for the supplier, plus a sincere apology and a root-cause fix. Reversing the debit alone leaves him out of pocket and embarrassed; making him file formally delays an obvious remedy.

bank.question: An e-commerce company refunded a customer in full within 24 hours for a damaged mixer grinder. However, the agent said on the call, "Customers like you always find something to complain about." The customer still posted an angry review. Which fairness dimension failed?
options: Fair treatment
Fair outcome
Fair process
None, because the refund was full and fast
bank.explanation: The outcome (full refund) and process (24 hours) were fair, but the customer was treated with disrespect. Customers judge interpersonal treatment separately, and disrespect alone can turn a well-resolved case into a detractor.

bank.question: A customer in Karachi writes on the company's official WhatsApp: "Mera bill is month double kyun aya hai? Koi batayega?" Brand guidelines allow replies in English, Urdu or Roman Urdu. What is the best approach for the reply?
options: Reply in formal English, because written replies should always be in English
Reply in simple Roman Urdu, matching the customer, without billing jargon
Ask the customer to call the helpline because WhatsApp is not for billing
Send a link to the full tariff document in English
bank.explanation: Following the customer's language and keeping explanations simple reduces effort and misunderstanding, and is within the brand guidelines. Insisting on English or redirecting to another channel adds effort; a tariff document does not answer why this bill doubled.

bank.question: A bank plans to close pension counters at urban branches within three months and require pensioners to use the app, to cut costs. Many pensioners are elderly and some have low literacy. Which approach best balances cost and CX?
options: Proceed as planned; pensioners will adapt once counters close
Cancel the digital plan entirely, since older customers generally cannot use apps safely
Keep counters open indefinitely but stop promoting the app
Phase it: assisted onboarding, simple guides in customers' languages and a retained assisted route
bank.explanation: Good omnichannel design guides customers to digital where it helps while keeping an assisted route for those excluded. Forcing the change risks hardship and complaints; assuming older customers cannot use apps is a stereotype; abandoning promotion loses the cost and convenience benefits.

bank.question: A woman customer at a busy branch counter hesitates and lowers her voice when asked about a loan for a family medical emergency. What should the officer do?
options: Offer to continue at a private desk, or with a female colleague if she prefers
Ask her to speak up so the details can be recorded correctly
Ask her to return with a male family member
Continue at the counter but speak faster to save her time
bank.explanation: Offering privacy, and a female colleague if preferred, respects dignity and sensitive circumstances without making assumptions. Asking her to speak up publicly, or to bring a male relative, is inappropriate; rushing her does not address the discomfort.

bank.question: A customer is quoted a USD 0 fee for an international transfer on the app's fee screen, but the branch charges USD 3 for the same transfer. The customer complains about being misled. What is the best response?
options: Explain that branch fees legitimately differ from app fees and charge the USD 3
Refund the USD 3 only if the customer escalates to a supervisor
Honour the quoted fee, fix the wrong information at source and check for others
Advise the customer to use the app in future and close the case
bank.explanation: The customer relied on information the bank provided. Honouring it, correcting the source and checking for others is fair and fixes the omnichannel inconsistency. Charging regardless or refunding only on escalation rewards persistence rather than fairness.

bank.question: From 1,000 NPS responses: 150 scored 10, 170 scored 9, 200 scored 8, 130 scored 7 and 350 scored 0–6. What is the NPS?
bank.explanation: Promoters = 150 + 170 = 320 (32%). Detractors = 350 (35%). NPS = 32 − 35 = −3. +3 reverses the subtraction; +32 is the promoter share only; −35 is the detractor share only.

bank.question: A telecom has 400 NPS responses: 140 promoters, 120 passives, 140 detractors. A network fix is expected to move 40 detractors to passives, with no other change. What would the new NPS be?
bank.explanation: Current NPS = 35% − 35% = 0. After the change: promoters 140 (35%), detractors 100 (25%), so NPS = 35 − 25 = +10. +20 wrongly treats the moved customers as promoters; +35 ignores detractors.

bank.question: Team A measures effort on a 1–5 scale where 1 means very low effort; its average is 2.1. Team B uses a 1–7 agreement scale for "It was easy to handle my issue"; its average is 5.6. A manager says Team A performs worse because its score is lower. What is correct?
options: The manager is right, because 2.1 is lower than 5.6
Team B is worse because its score is further from the maximum
They cannot be compared directly: the scales and directions differ
Both teams perform the same once both scores are converted to percentages of the maximum
bank.explanation: On Team A's scale lower is better; on Team B's higher is better, and the ranges differ. Both results look fairly positive, but they cannot be ranked against each other. Simple percentage conversion does not fix the different questions and directions.

bank.question: In a month, a contact centre records 12,500 contacts relating to 5,000 unique issues. For 1,100 of those issues, the customer contacted again about the same issue within 7 days. What is FCR using the repeat-contact method?
